john-of-islay.s: John of Islay was a chief of Clan Donald, descended from Somerled, who was the first to style himself Lord of the Isles (Dominus Insularum). Through marriages to Amy MacRuari and to a daughter of Robert II of Scotland he built a Gaelic lordship spanning the Hebrides and the…

john-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg.s: John, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, was a son of Otto the Child. When he and his brother Albert the Tall divided the duchy in 1269, John received Lüneburg and became the first prince of the Principality of Lüneburg.

john-of-montfort.s: John of Montfort was lord of Tyre in the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem from 1270, succeeding his father Philip of Montfort, who was murdered by an Assassin. He kept the city's trade alive through truces with the Mamluk sultans.

john-of-neuilly.s: John of Neuilly was a Frankish knight and hereditary marshal of the Principality of Achaea. Around 1220 he received a fief at the entrance to the Mani peninsula in the Peloponnese and built the castle of Passavant to control the Maniots.

john-penn-governor.s: John Penn was a grandson of William Penn and a proprietor of Pennsylvania. He served as lieutenant governor of the Province of Pennsylvania and of the Lower Counties on Delaware from 1763 to 1771 and again from 1773 to 1776, making him the last colonial governor before the…

john-sevier.s: John Sevier was a frontier soldier and politician who fought at the Battle of Kings Mountain in 1780. He served as governor of the breakaway State of Franklin from 1785 until it collapsed in 1788.

john-smith-explorer.s: John Smith was an English soldier and explorer who helped found Jamestown in 1607 and led the Virginia colony as president of its council in 1608 and 1609. His leadership kept the struggling settlement alive through its early hardships.

john-smith-missionary.s: John Smith was an English missionary of the London Missionary Society who served enslaved people in Demerara from 1817. After the Demerara rebellion of 1823 he was accused of encouraging the rising, court-martialled and sentenced to death, and died in prison in 1824 before a…

john-vii-count-of-nassau-siegen.s: John VII, Count of Nassau-Siegen, known as John the Middle, received Siegen after the death of his father, John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg, in 1606. A leading Calvinist military reformer, he wrote on the drill methods of the Dutch army and founded a military academy at Siegen in…

john-viii-count-of-nassau-siegen.s: John VIII, Count of Nassau-Siegen, known as John the Younger, was a son of John VII. He converted to Catholicism in 1612 and served Spain as a general.

john-wentworth-governor.s: John Wentworth was the last royal governor of the Province of New Hampshire, appointed in 1767 in succession to his uncle Benning Wentworth. He granted the charter of Dartmouth College in 1769 and built roads, but fled in 1775 as the American Revolution began.

john-william-friso.s: John William Friso was prince of Nassau-Dietz and stadtholder of Friesland and Groningen. In 1702 he inherited part of William III's estate and took the title Prince of Orange, though the inheritance was disputed with Prussia.

john-winthrop.s: John Winthrop was an English Puritan lawyer who led the Winthrop Fleet of about 1,000 settlers to Massachusetts in 1630 and founded Boston. Governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony for most of its first two decades, he described the colony as a 'city upon a hill'.

jon-sigurdsson.s: Jón Sigurðsson was an Icelandic scholar and politician who led the nineteenth-century movement for Iceland's self-government from Copenhagen. As president of the Althing he pressed Denmark for home rule, and the constitution of 1874 granted Iceland control over its own affairs.

jonathan-trumbull.s: Jonathan Trumbull was governor of the Connecticut Colony from 1769 to 1784 and the only colonial governor to support the American Revolution. Under him Connecticut kept its charter government and supplied the Continental Army with food, cattle and munitions, earning the name…

jonker-afrikaner.s: Jonker Afrikaner was the leader of the Oorlam Afrikaners, a horse-riding, gun-using community from the Cape frontier. Around 1823 he moved north into central Namibia at the invitation of the Nama to fight the Herero, and by about 1840 settled at Windhoek.

jorge-de-figueiredo-correia.s: Jorge de Figueiredo Correia was a Portuguese royal official and treasury scribe to whom King John III granted the Captaincy of Ilhéus in Brazil in 1534. He never went to the colony, governing through his lieutenant Francisco Romero, who founded the town of São Jorge dos Ilhéus.

jose-antonio-aguirre.s: José Antonio Aguirre was a Basque Nationalist Party politician and former footballer who became the first lehendakari, or president, of the autonomous Basque government. He took his oath under the oak of Guernica on 7 October 1936, during the Spanish Civil War.

jose-de-anchieta.s: José de Anchieta was a Spanish-born Jesuit missionary from Tenerife who worked in Brazil from 1553. With Manuel da Nóbrega he founded the mission that became São Paulo in 1554, and he wrote a grammar of the Tupi language and religious plays.

jose-de-antequera-y-castro.s: José de Antequera y Castro was a Panamanian-born judge of the Audiencia of Charcas sent to investigate the governor of Paraguay in 1721. He took over the governorship himself, backed by settlers who resented the Jesuits' control of Guaraní labour, and defied the viceroy,…

jose-de-escandon.s: José de Escandón was a Spanish military officer and colonial administrator commissioned by the viceroy of New Spain in 1746 to colonise the Gulf coast north of Tampico. From 1748 he founded more than twenty towns and missions between the Pánuco and Nueces rivers, creating the…

jose-fernando-de-abascal.s: José Fernando de Abascal was a Spanish officer who served as viceroy of Peru from 1806 to 1816. Making Lima the centre of royalist resistance to the Spanish American independence movements, he sent armies against the patriots in Upper Peru, Quito and Chile, where his troops…

jose-gaspar-rodriguez-de-francia.s: José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia was a lawyer and theologian who led Paraguay after independence. He became dictator in 1814 and perpetual dictator in 1816, ruling as El Supremo until his death in 1840.

jose-hilario-lopez.s: José Hilario López was a Colombian general and Liberal politician who served as president of the Republic of New Granada from 1849 to 1853. His government carried out major liberal reforms, abolishing slavery from 1 January 1852, expelling the Jesuits and separating more of…

jose-joaquin-de-olmedo.s: José Joaquín de Olmedo was an Ecuadorian poet and statesman who wrote the ode La victoria de Junín in honour of Simón Bolívar. After Guayaquil threw off Spanish rule on 9 October 1820 he headed the government of the Free Province of Guayaquil until Bolívar annexed it to Gran…

jose-maria-barrera.s: José María Barrera was a Maya rebel leader in the Caste War of Yucatán. In 1850 he promoted the cult of the Speaking Cross at a cenote in eastern Yucatán, which gave the rebels divine guidance in war.

jose-miguel-carrera.s: José Miguel Carrera was a Chilean independence leader who seized power in a series of coups from 1811. He introduced a provisional constitution, the first national flag and the first press during the Patria Vieja.

jose-mujica.s: José Mujica was a former Tupamaro guerrilla, imprisoned for some thirteen years under military rule, who became president of Uruguay for the Frente Amplio from 2010 to 2015. His government legalised same-sex marriage and the production and sale of cannabis.

josef-friedrich-matthes.s: Josef Friedrich Matthes was a German journalist and Rhenish separatist who led the provisional government of the Rhenish Republic in Koblenz in 1923, alongside Hans Adam Dorten. The republic depended on the tolerance of French occupation forces and collapsed within months.

josef-terboven.s: Josef Terboven was a Nazi Party official and Gauleiter of Essen whom Hitler appointed Reich Commissioner for Norway in April 1940. He held real power over the occupied country from Oslo, working with Vidkun Quisling's Nasjonal Samling while repressing resistance through…

joseph-bonaparte.s: Joseph Bonaparte was the elder brother of Napoleon, who made him king of Naples in 1806. In Naples he abolished feudalism, closed monasteries and introduced French administration.

joseph-chatoyer.s: Joseph Chatoyer was paramount chief of the Garifuna, or Black Caribs, of Saint Vincent. He resisted British encroachment on Garifuna lands in the First Carib War and, allied with revolutionary France, led the Second Carib War of 1795.

joseph-de-saint-ovide-de-brouillan.s: Joseph de Saint-Ovide de Brouillan was a French officer who served in Acadia and Newfoundland before becoming governor of Île Royale, present-day Cape Breton Island, from 1717 to 1739. He oversaw the growth of Louisbourg as a fortified port and fishing centre, trading with…

joseph-dudley.s: Joseph Dudley was a Massachusetts-born colonial official, son of Governor Thomas Dudley. After the Massachusetts charter was revoked, he headed the interim government of New England from 1686 until Edmund Andros arrived.

joseph-frederick-wallet-desbarres.s: Joseph Frederick Wallet DesBarres was a Swiss-born military engineer and cartographer whose Atlantic Neptune charted the coasts of North America. In 1784 he became the first lieutenant governor of the new Colony of Cape Breton Island and founded Sydney as its capital in 1785.

joseph-nasi.s: Joseph Nasi was a Portuguese-born Jewish financier and diplomat who rose to great influence at the Ottoman court under Selim II. In 1566 the sultan made him duke of Naxos and the Archipelago after deposing its last Crispo duke, and he ruled the islands through a deputy.

joseph-francois-dupleix.s: Joseph François Dupleix was governor-general of French India at Pondicherry from 1742 to 1754. During the Carnatic wars he intervened in the succession disputes of the Carnatic and Hyderabad, raising sepoy armies and installing allied rulers, and briefly made France the…

josephine-de-beauharnais.s: Joséphine de Beauharnais was born at Trois-Îlets on Martinique into a planter family. Widowed when her husband Alexandre de Beauharnais was guillotined in 1794, she married Napoleon Bonaparte in 1796 and became Empress of the French in 1804, until their divorce in 1810.

josiah-zion-gumede.s: Josiah Zion Gumede was a Zimbabwean politician of Abel Muzorewa's United African National Council. Under the internal settlement he became the first and only president of Zimbabwe Rhodesia from June to December 1979, a largely ceremonial post.

josif-rajacic.s: Josif Rajačić was a Serbian Orthodox churchman, metropolitan of Karlovci from 1842. At the May Assembly of Sremski Karlovci in 1848 the Serbs of southern Hungary elected him patriarch and proclaimed the Serbian Vojvodina.

jovan-dragas.s: Jovan Dragaš was a Serbian nobleman, son of the sebastokrator Dejan and nephew of Stefan Dušan. After Dušan's death in 1355 he and his brother Konstantin Dragaš built an autonomous lordship in north-eastern Macedonia, around Kumanovo, Kyustendil and Strumica.

jozef-ostrowski.s: Józef Ostrowski was a Polish landowner and conservative politician who had sat in the Russian State Council. In 1917 he became one of the three members of the Regency Council of the Kingdom of Poland, alongside Archbishop Aleksander Kakowski and Prince Zdzisław Lubomirski.

juan-araneta.s: Juan Araneta was a sugar planter and revolutionary general from Bago on Negros Island in the Philippines. With Aniceto Lacson he led the rising of 5 November 1898 that drove out the Spanish garrison within days and set up the Republic of Negros.

juan-bautista-de-anza.s: Juan Bautista de Anza was a frontier officer of New Spain, born in Sonora, who led overland expeditions to Alta California in 1774 and 1775–1776, bringing the settlers who founded San Francisco. As governor of New Mexico from 1778 to 1787 he defeated the Comanche leader Cuerno…

juan-calfucura.s: Juan Calfucurá was a Mapuche leader who crossed from Araucanía to the Argentine pampas around 1835 and seized control of the Salinas Grandes salt flats. From there he built a powerful confederation of pampas peoples that raided the Argentine frontier for decades.

juan-carlos-i.s: Juan Carlos I was king of Spain from 1975 to 2014. Francisco Franco named him as his successor in 1969, but after Franco's death he backed the transition to democracy with Prime Minister Adolfo Suárez, leading to the constitution of 1978.

juan-de-garay.s: Juan de Garay was a Basque-born conquistador who served in Peru and Paraguay. From Asunción he founded Santa Fe in 1573 and refounded Buenos Aires in 1580, decades after Pedro de Mendoza's first settlement had been abandoned.

juan-de-onate.s: Juan de Oñate was a conquistador born in New Spain who led settlers, soldiers and Franciscans up the Camino Real in 1598 and founded the province of Santa Fe de Nuevo México. He became its first governor, but his brutal punishment of Acoma Pueblo in 1599 and costly failures…

juan-manuel-rodriguez.s: Juan Manuel Rodríguez was a Salvadoran independence leader who took part in the San Salvador uprising of 1811. After Central America left the Mexican Empire, he became the first head of state of El Salvador within the Federal Republic of Central America in 1824.

juan-mora-fernandez.s: Juan Mora Fernández was a Costa Rican teacher and politician who became the first head of state of Costa Rica within the Federal Republic of Central America, governing from 1824 to 1833. His administration kept the state out of the federal wars, encouraged coffee cultivation,…

juan-nepomuceno-almonte.s: Juan Nepomuceno Almonte was a Mexican soldier and diplomat, son of the independence leader José María Morelos. A conservative, he supported French intervention and headed the regency that governed in the name of the Second Mexican Empire from 1863 until Maximilian of Austria…

juan-nunez-i-de-lara.s: Juan Núñez I de Lara was a Castilian magnate of the powerful House of Lara. Through his marriage to Teresa Álvarez de Azagra he became lord of Albarracín, an independent lordship between Castile and Aragon.

juan-pablo-duarte.s: Juan Pablo Duarte was the leading founding father of the Dominican Republic. In 1838 he founded the secret society La Trinitaria to organise resistance to Haitian rule.

juan-peron.s: Juan Perón was an Argentine army officer who rose to power as labour minister after the 1943 coup and was elected president in 1946. With his wife Eva Perón he built a mass movement based on trade unions, industrialisation and social welfare.

juan-pio-de-tristan.s: Juan Pío de Tristán was a wealthy Arequipa landowner and royalist general who served as the last viceroy of Peru briefly in 1824, after the Battle of Ayacucho. He later accepted independence and became president of the South Peruvian Republic within Andrés de Santa Cruz's…

juan-rafael-mora-porras.s: Juan Rafael Mora Porras was a coffee merchant and president of Costa Rica from 1849 to 1859. He led the Central American coalition that defeated the American filibuster William Walker in Nicaragua in 1856 and 1857, and is honoured as a national hero.

juan-vicente-gomez.s: Juan Vicente Gómez was a soldier from the Andes who seized power in Venezuela in 1908 and ruled as dictator until his death in 1935. His regime crushed opposition, centralised the state and built a professional army.

jules-gros.s: Jules Gros was a French journalist and geographer whom adventurers in Paris named president for life of the Republic of Counani in 1886. The republic was proclaimed in territory disputed between France and Brazil in the Guiana region, but Gros never visited it, and the state…

julia-domna.s: Julia Domna was a Roman empress, daughter of the high priest of the sun god at Emesa in Syria. She married Septimius Severus and was the mother of the emperors Caracalla and Geta, and she accompanied Severus on his campaign in Britain against the Caledonians.

julian-grenier.s: Julian Grenier was lord of Sidon and Beaufort in the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem. His raid into Mongol-held territory in 1260 provoked a Mongol attack that sacked Sidon.

julien-fedon.s: Julien Fédon was a free coloured planter of French descent on Grenada. Inspired by revolutionary France, he led the rebellion of 1795 to 1796, which won the support of enslaved people, held most of the island and killed the British lieutenant governor and other hostages.

julius-civilis.s: Julius Civilis was a Batavian noble and Roman auxiliary commander who led the Batavian revolt of 69 to 70 CE during the civil wars of the Year of the Four Emperors. Joined by the Cananefates, Frisii and Treveri, the rebels destroyed several Roman forts on the Rhine.

julius-echter-von-mespelbrunn.s: Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn was prince-bishop of Würzburg from 1573 to 1617. A leading figure of the Counter-Reformation, he forced Protestants to convert or leave, refounded the University of Würzburg in 1582 and built the Juliusspital hospital.

julius-sundblom.s: Julius Sundblom was a journalist and politician from the Åland Islands who led the movement for reunion with Sweden after Finnish independence. When the League of Nations awarded Åland to Finland with guaranteed autonomy in 1921, he became the first speaker of its parliament,…

julius-von-pflug.s: Julius von Pflug was a German humanist and Catholic theologian who sought reconciliation with the Lutherans and helped draft the Augsburg Interim of 1548. Elected bishop of Naumburg in 1541, he was kept out by the Lutheran Nicholas of Amsdorf until 1547.

junaid-khan.s: Junaid Khan was a Turkmen tribal leader of the Yomut who became the real power in the Khanate of Khiva from 1918. After the Red Army and the Young Khivans overthrew the khanate in 1920, he fought the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic and later Soviet rule as a leader of the…

juozas-ambrazevicius.s: Juozas Ambrazevičius was a Lithuanian literary scholar who served as acting prime minister of the Provisional Government of Lithuania in June to August 1941, after the uprising against Soviet rule at the start of the German invasion. The Germans dissolved the government, and…

jupiter-latiaris.s: Jupiter Latiaris was the form of Jupiter worshipped as the shared god of the Latin peoples at his sanctuary on the Alban Mount, now Monte Cavo, near the site of Alba Longa. His annual festival, the Feriae Latinae, gathered the Latin communities for a common sacrifice.

juqu-anzhou.s: Juqu Anzhou was a prince of the Northern Liang, brother of its last ruler Juqu Mujian. After Northern Wei conquered Northern Liang in 439, he and his brother Juqu Wuhui fled west and seized Gaochang in 442.

juqu-mujian.s: Juqu Mujian was the last ruler of the Northern Liang, one of the Sixteen Kingdoms in the Hexi Corridor, succeeding his father Juqu Mengxun in 433. Northern Wei captured his capital Guzang and took him prisoner in 439, completing its unification of northern China.

jurgen-wullenwever.s: Jürgen Wullenwever was a Lübeck merchant who rose to power as a popular Lutheran leader and became mayor in 1533. He tried to restore Lübeck's dominance of Baltic trade by intervening in the Danish succession, leading the city into the Count's Feud of 1534 to 1536.

juscelino-kubitschek.s: Juscelino Kubitschek was a doctor and politician, governor of Minas Gerais, who served as president of Brazil from 1956 to 1961. Promising 'fifty years in five', he pushed rapid industrialisation, road building and the motor industry.

justan-iii.s: Justan III was a ruler of the Justanid dynasty of Daylam in the mountains of northern Iran. After 864 he supported the Zaydi Alavid dynasty of Tabaristan, helping establish Shia Islam among the Daylamites.

justo-rufino-barrios.s: Justo Rufino Barrios was a Guatemalan general who led the Liberal Revolution of 1871 and ruled as president from 1873 to 1885. He expropriated church lands, expelled the Jesuits and built roads, railways and schools.

juvenal-habyarimana.s: Juvénal Habyarimana was a Rwandan army officer who seized power in a coup in 1973 and ruled a one-party state for over twenty years. The Rwandan Patriotic Front invaded in 1990, and he signed the Arusha Accords in 1993.

jayabaya.s: Jayabaya was king of Kediri in East Java in the mid 12th century. An inscription of 1135 records his victory over Janggala with the words Panjalu jayati, Panjalu is victorious, uniting the realm Airlangga had divided.

jinheung-of-silla.s: Jinheung was king of Silla from 540 to 576 and its greatest early conqueror. Allied with Baekje, he took the Han river valley from Goguryeo and then seized it from Baekje in 553, gaining access to the Yellow Sea.

john-ii-of-aragon.s: John II was King of Navarre by marriage from 1425 and King of Aragon from 1458 until his death. His conflict with his son Charles of Viana and with the Catalan institutions led to the Catalan Civil War of 1462 to 1472, which he eventually won.

jun-of-gojoseon.s: Jun was the last king of the Gija line of Gojoseon in northern Korea, according to Chinese and Korean historical tradition. Around 194 BCE he was overthrown by Wiman, a refugee from the Chinese state of Yan whom he had employed to guard his frontier.

john-lambton-1st-earl-of-durham.s: John Lambton, 1st Earl of Durham, was a British Whig statesman sent as governor-general of British North America after the rebellions of 1837–1838. His Report on the Affairs of British North America of 1839 recommended uniting Upper and Lower Canada, partly to assimilate…

james-bruce-8th-earl-of-elgin.s: James Bruce, 8th Earl of Elgin, was a British colonial administrator who served as governor-general of the Province of Canada from 1847 to 1854. By signing the Rebellion Losses Bill in 1849 despite riots that burned the parliament in Montreal, he confirmed responsible government.

judicial-committee-of-the-privy-council.n: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
judicial-committee-of-the-privy-council.s: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, set up in London in 1833, served as the final court of appeal for British colonies and dominions. Its rulings settled many imperial disputes, among them Sobhuza II's unsuccessful land case from Swaziland in 1926 and the 1927 award…

joanna-i-of-naples.s: Joanna I was queen of Naples and countess of Provence from 1343 to 1382. Her reign was troubled by the murder of her first husband and wars with Hungary.

jai-singh-ii.s: Jai Singh II was the Kachhwaha raja of Amber in Rajasthan from 1699 to 1743 and a leading noble of the late Mughal Empire. In 1727 he founded the new capital of Jaipur, laid out on a grid plan.

jamshid-bin-abdullah.s: Jamshid bin Abdullah was the last sultan of Zanzibar. He succeeded his father in July 1963 and reigned as constitutional monarch when Zanzibar became independent in December 1963, but was overthrown by the Zanzibar Revolution of January 1964, which created the People's…

josef-wegner.s: Josef Wegner is an American Egyptologist at the University of Pennsylvania who has directed excavations at South Abydos, notably at the mortuary complex of Senusret III. In 2014 his team found there the tomb of Senebkay, a previously unknown king of around 1650 BCE, giving…

jalal-al-din-mangburni.s: Jalal al-Din Mingburnu was the last ruler of the Khwarazmian Empire. After his father's defeat by Genghis Khan he fought on, winning at Parwan in 1221 before being routed on the Indus.

jordanes.s: Jordanes was a 6th-century Roman historian of Gothic descent writing in Constantinople. His Getica, completed around 551, abridges the lost Gothic history of Cassiodorus and is the main surviving account of the origins and early history of the Goths.

johann-gottlieb-christaller.s: Johann Gottlieb Christaller was a German missionary and linguist of the Basel Mission who worked on the Gold Coast, now Ghana, from 1853. Based largely at Akropong, he translated the Bible into Akuapem Twi, completing it in 1871, and wrote a grammar and a large dictionary of…

junipero-serra.s: Junípero Serra was a Spanish Franciscan friar from Majorca who founded the first nine of the 21 Spanish missions of Alta California, beginning with San Diego in 1769. He had earlier worked as a missionary in Mexico's Sierra Gorda.

jats.s: The Jats are an agricultural community of north-western India and Pakistan, living mainly in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh. In the 17th and 18th centuries Jat peasants rose against Mughal rule, and leaders such as Churaman and Suraj Mal built the kingdom…

jabbok.s: The Jabbok, now the Zarqa River, is a river of Jordan and the second largest tributary of the Jordan, flowing from near Amman north and then west to join it north of the Dead Sea. In the Iron Age its upper course bounded the kingdom of Ammon.

jinsha-site.s: The Jinsha site is an archaeological site in western Chengdu, Sichuan, discovered in 2001 and dating from about 1200 to 500 BCE. It is thought to have been the centre of the Shu culture after the decline of Sanxingdui, and has yielded gold, jade, bronze and ivory objects,…

jetavanaramaya.s: The Jetavanaramaya is a Buddhist stupa in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, begun by King Mahasena in the 3rd century CE. Built of brick and originally about 122 metres high, it was among the tallest structures of the ancient world.

james-moore-carolina-governor.s: James Moore was an English colonist and governor of the Province of Carolina from 1700 to 1703. In 1702 he led an unsuccessful siege of Spanish St Augustine during Queen Anne's War.

justo-jose-de-urquiza.s: Justo José de Urquiza was an Argentine general and politician, long governor of Entre Ríos. He broke with Juan Manuel de Rosas and defeated him at Caseros in 1852, then sponsored the Constitution of 1853 and served as first constitutional president of the Argentine…

javier-milei.s: Javier Milei is an Argentine economist and politician who became president of Argentina in December 2023. A libertarian television commentator first elected to Congress in 2021, he won the presidency amid inflation above 100 per cent a year, promising to cut back the state…

jublains.s: Jublains is a village in the Mayenne department of north-western France, on the site of Noviodunum Diablintum, the Roman capital of the Gallic Diablintes. Its remains include a temple, baths, a theatre and an unusual late Roman fortified building, probably a store for military…

jalaun-district.s: Jalaun district is a district in the Bundelkhand region of Uttar Pradesh, India, south of the Yamuna, with its headquarters at Orai. In the 18th century the area came under Maratha rule, and Jalaun became a Maratha principality that lapsed to the British in 1840.

jubba-river.s: The Jubba is a river of southern Somalia, formed by the Ganale and Dawa rivers that rise in the Ethiopian Highlands, which flows south across Somalia to the Indian Ocean near Kismayo. With the Shabelle it waters the fertile inter-riverine region, home to farming Somali clans…

jammu.s: Jammu is a city on the Tawi river in the foothills of the Himalaya, the winter capital of the Indian union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, and the name of the surrounding region. It was the seat of the Dogra Rajas, who under the Sikh Empire absorbed the neighbouring hill…

jos-plateau.s: The Jos Plateau is an upland region in central Nigeria, rising to over 1,200 metres, with the city of Jos at its centre. It is home to many small ethnic groups who long resisted the 19th-century jihad states around it.

johannes-hoffmann.s: Johannes Hoffmann was a German Social Democratic politician who became Minister-President of Bavaria in March 1919, after the murder of Kurt Eisner. When the Bavarian Soviet Republic was proclaimed in April, his government withdrew to Bamberg and called in government troops…

joseph-kasavubu.s: Joseph Kasavubu was the first president of the Republic of the Congo (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), from independence in 1960 to 1965. As leader of ABAKO, a party of the Bakongo, he campaigned for independence.

johnny-briceno.s: Johnny Briceño is a Belizean politician, leader of the People's United Party and Prime Minister of Belize since November 2020. He had served as deputy prime minister under Said Musa.

john-doukas-megas-doux.s: John Doukas was a Byzantine general and admiral, brother-in-law of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos. As megas doux, commander of the fleet, he fought the Turkish emir Tzachas and recovered Crete and Cyprus from rebels in the early 1090s.

jajpur.s: Jajpur is a town on the Baitarani river in Odisha, eastern India, and headquarters of the district of the same name. It was a capital of the Bhauma-Kara and Somavamshi dynasties and is an important Hindu pilgrimage centre, with the temple of the goddess Viraja (Biraja).

jangladesh.s: Jangladesh, 'the land of scrub forest', was the old name of the arid region of northern Rajasthan around modern Bikaner. Before the late 15th century it was held by Jat clans and by Bhati and other Rajputs.

jaja-of-opobo.s: Jaja of Opobo was a merchant king in the Niger Delta. Born in Igboland and sold as a boy into slavery in Bonny, he rose to head the Anna Pepple trading house and in 1869 founded the Kingdom of Opobo, which took control of much of the palm oil trade.

joao-figueiredo.s: João Figueiredo was a Brazilian general and the last president of the military dictatorship, serving from 1979 to 1985. He continued the gradual opening begun by Ernesto Geisel, granting an amnesty in 1979 and allowing the return of a multi-party system, and handed power to a…

jan-willem-janssens.s: Jan Willem Janssens was a Dutch general and colonial governor. As governor of the Cape Colony for the Batavian Republic from 1803 he was defeated by the British in 1806, and as governor-general of the Dutch East Indies under Napoleon he surrendered Java to a British invasion…

james-elphinstone-erskine.s: James Elphinstone Erskine was a British naval officer. As commodore of the Australia Station he proclaimed a British protectorate over the south-eastern coast of New Guinea at Port Moresby in November 1884, the origin of British New Guinea and later Papua.

james-chalmers-missionary.s: James Chalmers was a Scottish missionary of the London Missionary Society who worked first on Rarotonga in the Cook Islands and from 1877 in New Guinea. He travelled widely along the southern coast, helped the British when they proclaimed their protectorate in 1884, and was…

jeremie.s: Jérémie is a port town on the northern coast of the south-western peninsula of Haiti, capital of the Grand'Anse department. In the colony of Saint-Domingue it was a coffee-growing district, and in September 1793 British troops from Jamaica landed there at the invitation of…

james-mancham.s: Sir James Mancham was a Seychellois politician, founder of the Seychelles Democratic Party, who served as chief minister and then as the first president of the Seychelles at independence in 1976. He was overthrown in a coup by France-Albert René in June 1977 while abroad, and…

john-coakley-lettsom.s: John Coakley Lettsom was an English physician and philanthropist born to a Quaker family on Jost Van Dyke in the British Virgin Islands. He freed the slaves he inherited, built a large practice in London and founded the Medical Society of London in 1773.

jost-van-dyke.s: Jost Van Dyke is one of the four main islands of the British Virgin Islands, lying north-west of Tortola and named after a Dutch privateer. In the 18th century it was home to a small Quaker community, and the physician John Coakley Lettsom and the architect William Thornton…

jan-van-eyck.s: Jan van Eyck was an Early Netherlandish painter who worked at Bruges as court painter to Philip the Good, duke of Burgundy. He perfected oil painting techniques that allowed great detail and luminous colour, seen in the Ghent Altarpiece, completed in 1432, and the Arnolfini…

jinja.s: Jinja is a city in eastern Uganda on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, near the point where the Victoria Nile leaves the lake. Founded as a British administrative and trading centre in 1901, it grew into an industrial town after the Owen Falls Dam was completed in 1954.

jilin-city.s: Jilin is a city in Jilin province in north-eastern China, on the Songhua River. Its area was a centre of the ancient kingdom of Buyeo, and from the 17th century the city grew as a Qing shipbuilding base and garrison, giving its name to the province.

jilin.s: Jilin is a province of north-eastern China, bordering North Korea and Russia, with its capital at Changchun. Its lands were part of the ancient kingdoms of Buyeo, Goguryeo and Balhae, and later of Manchuria under the Qing dynasty, which long restricted Han Chinese settlement…

juan-de-salcedo.s: Juan de Salcedo was a Spanish conquistador, grandson of Miguel López de Legazpi, who led many of the early Spanish expeditions in Luzon. In 1571–1572 he explored and subdued the Ilocos coast and Pangasinan, and in 1574 he helped defend Manila against the Chinese corsair Limahong.

john-d-sloat.s: John Drake Sloat was a United States Navy officer who commanded the Pacific Squadron at the start of the Mexican–American War. On 7 July 1846 he landed at Monterey and claimed Alta California for the United States, ending the California Republic.

john-c-fremont.s: John C. Frémont was an American explorer, army officer and politician whose expeditions mapped much of the American West in the 1840s.

johann-froben.s: Johann Froben was a printer and publisher in Basel and one of the leading printers of the Renaissance. He published the works of Erasmus, who lived in his house, including the first published Greek New Testament in 1516, and employed Hans Holbein the Younger to design title…

juan-contreras-y-roman.s: Juan Contreras y Román was a Spanish general and federal republican. In July 1873 he joined the Cantonal rebellion at Cartagena, becoming commander of the canton's forces and of the fleet seized there, which raided Alicante, Almería and other ports for supplies.

jian-an-poetry.s: Jian'an poetry is the poetry written in China during the Jian'an era (196–220) at the end of the Han dynasty, centred on the court of Cao Cao. Its leading poets were Cao Cao, his sons Cao Pi and Cao Zhi, and the Seven Scholars of Jian'an.

jose-basco-y-vargas.s: José Basco y Vargas was a Spanish naval officer who served as governor-general of the Philippines from 1778 to 1787. He sought to make the colony pay for itself, founding the Economic Society of Friends of the Country in 1781 and introducing a government tobacco monopoly in 1782.

jose-rizal.s: José Rizal was a Filipino physician, writer and reformer, and the national hero of the Philippines. His novels Noli Me Tángere (1887) and El filibusterismo (1891) exposed the abuses of Spanish colonial rule and the friars.

jorge-amado.s: Jorge Amado was a Brazilian novelist from the cacao region of southern Bahia and one of the most widely read writers of Latin America. His early novels portrayed the violent struggle for the cacao lands, and later works such as Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon (1958) and Dona Flor…

jesuit-missions-of-chiquitos.s: The Jesuit Missions of Chiquitos were a group of mission towns founded among the Chiquitano and other peoples in the lowlands of eastern Bolivia between 1691 and 1760. The Jesuits organised the towns around large wooden churches and taught European music and crafts.

jesuit-missions-of-moxos.s: The Jesuit Missions of Moxos were mission towns founded from 1682 among the Moxo and other peoples of the seasonally flooded plains of the Beni, in northern Bolivia. They became a populous frontier of the Spanish empire facing Portuguese Mato Grosso across the Guaporé.

joao-dos-santos-missionary.s: João dos Santos was a Portuguese Dominican friar who served as a missionary in south-east Africa in the 1590s, living at Sofala and on the Zambezi. His book Ethiopia Oriental, published in 1609, describes the peoples and kingdoms of the region, including the court of the…

julius-asclepiodotus.s: Julius Asclepiodotus was a Roman praetorian prefect under the emperors Maximian and Constantius Chlorus, and consul in 292. In 296 he led part of the invasion force that recovered Britain from the usurper Allectus, landing under cover of fog and defeating and killing Allectus…

jalore.s: Jalore, or Jalor, is a town in south-western Rajasthan, India, below a granite hill crowned by one of the strongest forts of medieval Rajputana. Taken from the Paramaras around 1160 by the Chahamana Kirtipala, it was the capital of the Songara Chauhans until Alauddin Khalji…

juan-de-grijalva.s: Juan de Grijalva was a Spanish conquistador who led the second expedition from Cuba to the coast of Mexico in 1518. He sailed past Cozumel, fought at Champotón and followed the Gulf coast to the river now named after him, gathering the first reports of the Aztec Empire.

jejakabhukti.s: Jejakabhukti was the medieval name of the Bundelkhand region of central India, ruled by the Chandela dynasty from the 9th to the 13th century. Chandela inscriptions derive the name from Jeja, or Jayashakti, an early king of the line.

jayavarman-i.s: Jayavarman I was a king of Chenla in Cambodia in the second half of the 7th century, the last ruler to hold the kingdom together. His inscriptions show his authority reaching from the Mekong delta into southern Laos.

john-ross-cherokee-chief.s: John Ross (1790–1866) was Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation from 1828 until his death. Of mixed Scottish and Cherokee descent, he led the nation's legal and political resistance to removal, including its cases before the US Supreme Court, and opposed the Treaty of New…

juan-antonio-lavalleja.s: Juan Antonio Lavalleja (1784–1853) was a Uruguayan independence leader. A former officer of José Artigas, he led the Thirty-Three Orientals who landed from Buenos Aires in April 1825 to free the Banda Oriental from Brazil, starting the Cisplatine War.

joseph-gorres.s: Joseph Görres was a German writer and journalist from Koblenz. As a young radical he backed the French Revolution and the plan for a Cisrhenian Republic on the left bank of the Rhine in 1797, but he became disillusioned with French rule.

juan-pardo-explorer.s: Juan Pardo was a Spanish army officer who led two expeditions from Santa Elena, in present-day South Carolina, into the interior of the south-eastern United States between 1566 and 1568. Sent by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, he crossed the Carolinas into eastern Tennessee,…

jean-du-plessis-dossonville.s: Jean du Plessis d'Ossonville was a French nobleman who, with Charles Liénard de l'Olive, led the colonists sent by the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique to settle Guadeloupe in June 1635. The expedition landed in the north of Basse-Terre island, where the settlers suffered from…

james-monroe.s: James Monroe was the fifth President of the United States, serving from 1817 to 1825, after earlier posts as governor of Virginia, minister to France and Britain and secretary of state. His presidency saw the acquisition of Florida and the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, which warned…

john-cabot.s: John Cabot, born Giovanni Caboto in Italy, was a navigator who sailed from Bristol under a patent from Henry VII of England. In 1497 he reached the coast of North America, probably Newfoundland or Cape Breton, the first European known to do so since the Norse.

joseph-howe.s: Joseph Howe was a Nova Scotian journalist and politician. As editor of the Novascotian he won a landmark libel case in 1835 that strengthened freedom of the press, and he led the reformers who achieved responsible government in Nova Scotia in 1848, the first in the British…

john-clarke-baptist-minister.s: John Clarke was an English physician and Baptist minister who co-founded the colony of Rhode Island. With William Coddington he founded Portsmouth in 1638 and Newport in 1639, where he established one of the first Baptist churches in America.

john-batman.s: John Batman was an Australian grazier and explorer born in New South Wales who settled in Van Diemen's Land. In 1835 he crossed Bass Strait and signed a 'treaty' with Wurundjeri elders to acquire some 240,000 hectares around Port Phillip, which the colonial government declared…

john-pascoe-fawkner.s: John Pascoe Fawkner was an Australian pioneer, businessman and politician who helped found Melbourne in 1835. Raised in Van Diemen's Land, he sent a party on the schooner Enterprize to the Yarra River in 1835 and soon settled there himself.

james-river.s: The James River is a river in Virginia, United States, flowing about 560 kilometres from the Appalachian Mountains to Chesapeake Bay at Hampton Roads. Named after King James I, it was the site of Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in America, founded in 1607.

james-stirling-royal-navy-officer.s: James Stirling was a Royal Navy officer who founded the Swan River Colony in Western Australia. After exploring the Swan River in 1827, he persuaded the British government to establish a settlement, and in 1829 he founded Perth and Fremantle and became the colony's first…

jose-de-galvez.s: José de Gálvez was a Spanish official who, as visitor-general of New Spain from 1765 to 1771, drove the Bourbon reforms there: a tobacco monopoly, tighter tax collection, the expulsion of the Jesuits and the settlement of Alta California. As Minister of the Indies from 1776 he…

john-curtin.s: John Curtin was an Australian Labor politician and prime minister from 1941 until his death in 1945. After Japan entered the Second World War he declared that Australia looked to the United States, recalled troops from the Middle East and worked closely with General Douglas…

jacopo-i-da-carrara.s: Jacopo I da Carrara was a Paduan nobleman elected lord of Padua in 1318, when the commune sought a strong leader against Cangrande della Scala of Verona. His election founded the rule of the Carrara family, which lasted with interruptions until 1405.

jefferson-davis.s: Jefferson Davis was the only president of the Confederate States of America, from 1861 to 1865. A planter from Mississippi, he had served as an army officer, senator and US secretary of war.

january-uprising.s: The January Uprising was a Polish and Lithuanian insurrection against Russian rule, beginning in January 1863 in Congress Poland. Fought mainly by guerrilla bands under a secret national government, it was crushed by 1864.

jerome.s: Jerome was a Christian priest, scholar and Doctor of the Church, born in Dalmatia, who spent his later life as a monk in Bethlehem. His Latin translation of the Bible, later known as the Vulgate, became the standard text of the Western Church for over a thousand years.

jagaddipendra-narayan.s: Jagaddipendra Narayan was the last ruling Maharaja of Cooch Behar, succeeding as a child in 1922 and ruling in his own right from 1936. A noted sportsman, he served in the Second World War.

jonestown.s: Jonestown was a settlement in the forest of north-western Guyana founded by the American cult the Peoples Temple under Jim Jones. On 18 November 1978, after members killed US Congressman Leo Ryan and others at a nearby airstrip, 918 people died there and in Georgetown, most by…

joscelin-i-count-of-edessa.s: Joscelin I of Courtenay was count of Edessa from 1118 to 1131, after holding Turbessel as a vassal of his cousin Baldwin II. A tireless fighter against the Turks, he was captured at Harran in 1104 and again by Belek Ghazi in 1122, escaping the next year from the fortress of…

joan-ii-of-navarre.s: Joan II was queen of Navarre from 1328, the daughter of Louis X of France. Excluded from the French throne after her father's death, she was recognised in Navarre when the direct Capetian line ended, and ruled jointly with her husband Philip of Évreux.

judith-of-france.s: Judith was a daughter of the Frankish king Charles the Bald who married two kings of Wessex, Æthelwulf in 856 and then his son Æthelbald. Widowed, she eloped in 862 with Baldwin Iron Arm, and after her father reluctantly accepted the marriage Baldwin received lands around…

judith-of-flanders.s: Judith of Flanders was a daughter of Count Baldwin IV of Flanders who married Tostig Godwinson, Earl of Northumbria, and after his death in 1066 Welf IV, Duke of Bavaria. A patron of churches, she commissioned illuminated gospel books in England.

jakob-hannibal-i-of-hohenems.s: Jakob Hannibal I (1530–1587) was Count of Hohenems and a general in Spanish and papal service. A nephew of Pope Pius IV, he fought in Spain's wars in the Netherlands and the Mediterranean and married Ortensia Borromeo, sister of Charles Borromeo.

jagst.s: The Jagst is a river in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, about 190 km long and a right tributary of the Neckar. It rises at the eastern edge of the Swabian Jura, flows past Ellwangen and Crailsheim through the Hohenlohe plain and joins the Neckar at Bad Friedrichshall.

john-iv-count-of-katzenelnbogen.s: John IV (died 1444) was Count of Katzenelnbogen, a Rhineland county whose rulers drew great wealth from Rhine tolls. An account from his cellar at Rüsselsheim dated 1435, recording the purchase of Riesling vines, is the earliest known written mention of the grape.

johann-of-manderscheid-blankenheim.s: Johann of Manderscheid-Blankenheim (1538–1592) was Bishop of Strasbourg from 1569. A Catholic reformer in a largely Protestant city, he brought the Jesuits to Molsheim, where he founded a college in 1580 that later became a university.

john-duke-of-berry.s: John, Duke of Berry, was a son of King John II of France who held Berry, Auvergne and Poitou as appanages. He was a leading figure in the regency for his nephew Charles VI and one of the greatest art patrons of the Middle Ages, commissioning the illuminated manuscript known as…

johannes-trithemius.s: Johannes Trithemius was a German Benedictine abbot, humanist and scholar, abbot of Sponheim from 1483 and later of St James at Würzburg. He built Sponheim's library into one of the largest in Germany and wrote histories, catalogues of authors and the Steganographia and…

juliana-of-stolberg.s: Juliana of Stolberg was a German countess, daughter of Count Botho III of Stolberg, who married William, Count of Nassau-Dillenburg, in 1531. Of her many children, William the Silent led the Dutch Revolt and his brothers Louis, Adolf and Henry died in its cause, while John VI…

joan-countess-of-toulouse.s: Joan was the only child and heiress of Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse. Under the Treaty of Paris of 1229, which ended the Albigensian Crusade, she was married to Alphonse of Poitiers, brother of Louis IX.

joan-i-of-navarre.s: Joan I was Queen of Navarre and Countess of Champagne from 1274 until her death in 1305, the last of the house of Champagne. Her marriage in 1284 to the future Philip IV of France brought both lands under the French crown, and she founded the College of Navarre in Paris.

john-of-scotland-earl-of-huntingdon.n: John of Scotland, Earl of Huntingdon
john-of-scotland-earl-of-huntingdon.s: John of Scotland, known as John the Scot, was Earl of Huntingdon and, from 1232, Earl of Chester. The son of David, Earl of Huntingdon, and of Matilda, sister of Ranulf de Blondeville, he inherited Chester from his uncle.

jeronimo-de-aguilar.s: Jerónimo de Aguilar was a Spanish Franciscan who was shipwrecked on the coast of Yucatán in 1511 and lived among the Maya for eight years. Rescued by Hernán Cortés at Cozumel in 1519, he served as interpreter, and working with La Malinche, who translated between Nahuatl and…

jisan-dong-tombs.s: The Jisan-dong tombs are a group of over 700 burial mounds on a ridge above Goryeong in North Gyeongsang, South Korea, the royal cemetery of Daegaya. Excavations have found iron armour, gold crowns and tombs with many sacrificed attendants.

jinkaishu.s: The Jinkaishū was a law code issued in 1536 by Date Tanemune for the lands of the Date clan in southern Mutsu, in northern Japan. With 171 articles it is the longest of the house codes of the Sengoku warlords, dealing with criminal law, land, debts and relations between lords…

jerash.s: Jerash, the ancient Gerasa, is a city in northern Jordan whose Roman ruins are among the best preserved in the Middle East. A member of the Decapolis, it flourished from the 1st to the 3rd centuries CE, with colonnaded streets, an oval plaza, theatres, a temple of Artemis and…

jacob-nienhuys.s: Jacob Nienhuys was a Dutch tobacco planter who in 1863 began growing tobacco in the Sultanate of Deli, in north-eastern Sumatra, on land leased from the sultan. His success, especially with fine wrapper leaf for cigars, drew a rush of European planters to the region, and in…

janatha-vimukthi-peramuna.s: The Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), or People's Liberation Front, is a Marxist party in Sri Lanka founded in 1965 by Rohana Wijeweera. It led armed uprisings in 1971 and 1987–1989, both crushed by the state with heavy loss of life.

john-wise.s: John Wise was a Congregational minister of Ipswich, Massachusetts, known as an early advocate of democratic principles in church and state. In 1687 he led his town in refusing to pay a tax imposed by Sir Edmund Andros without an elected assembly, and was fined and imprisoned.

joey-smallwood.s: Joey Smallwood was a Newfoundland journalist and politician who led the campaign for confederation with Canada in the referendums of 1948. After Newfoundland became Canada's tenth province in 1949, he served as its first premier until 1972, pursuing industrial schemes and the…

joseph-ward.s: Sir Joseph Ward was Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1906 to 1912 and again from 1928 to 1930. A Liberal from Southland, he had been a leading minister under Richard Seddon, and at his request New Zealand was proclaimed a dominion in 1907.

judicael.s: Judicael was a king of Domnonée in northern Brittany in the 7th century, later venerated as a saint. According to the Chronicle of Fredegar, he came to the Frankish court at Clichy in 636 and made peace with Dagobert I, but declined to dine with the king.

junkers.s: Junkers was a German aircraft and engine manufacturer based in Dessau, founded by the engineer Hugo Junkers. It built early all-metal aircraft and the Ju 52 transport, and after its takeover by the Nazi state in 1935 produced warplanes such as the Ju 87 Stuka and Ju 88 bomber.

john-william-elector-palatine.s: John William was Duke of Jülich and Berg from 1679 and Elector Palatine from 1690. Because the Palatinate had been devastated by French armies in the Nine Years' War, he ruled from Düsseldorf, which he made a baroque court city with a famous painting gallery.

joanna-duchess-of-brabant.s: Joanna was Duchess of Brabant and Limburg from 1355 until her death in 1406. With her husband Wenceslaus of Luxembourg she swore the Joyous Entry charter in 1356 to secure recognition by the estates of Brabant.

joyous-entry-of-1356.s: The Joyous Entry was a charter of liberties granted in January 1356 by Duchess Joanna and Duke Wenceslaus to the estates of Brabant in return for recognition of their rule. It limited the duke's power to wage war, coin money and appoint foreigners to office, and allowed…

johann-weikhard-von-valvasor.s: Johann Weikhard von Valvasor was a Carniolan nobleman and polymath, born in Ljubljana. He travelled widely, set up a printing and engraving workshop at his castle of Bogenšperk and wrote The Glory of the Duchy of Carniola, published in 1689.

jablunkov-pass.s: The Jablunkov Pass is a mountain pass in the Western Beskids on the border between the Czech Republic and Slovakia, at about 550 metres. Since the Middle Ages it has carried a key route from Silesia and Moravia to Upper Hungary, now Slovakia, and it was fortified against the…

jelgava.s: Jelgava, known in German as Mitau, is a city in central Latvia on the Lielupe river. It grew around a castle built by the Livonian Order in 1265 and was the capital of the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia from 1578 to 1795, then of the Russian Governorate of Courland.

jarva-county.s: Järva County is a county in central Estonia, with its centre at Paide. The historic land of Järvamaa, called Jerwen in German, came under the Livonian Order in the 13th century, which built a castle at Weissenstein, now Paide.

jawor.s: Jawor is a town in Lower Silesia, Poland. It was the capital of a Piast duchy from 1274, ruled by Bolko I the Strict and his successors, and passed to the Bohemian crown in 1392.

john-george-duke-of-jagerndorf.s: John George of Brandenburg (1577–1624), a son of Elector Joachim Frederick of Brandenburg, was Duke of Jägerndorf (Krnov) in Silesia from 1607. A Calvinist, he commanded troops for the Bohemian estates in the revolt that opened the Thirty Years' War.

janusz-i-of-warsaw.s: Janusz I of Warsaw (c. 1346–1429), also called Janusz the Elder, was a Piast duke who ruled the northern and eastern part of Masovia from 1374.

jumieges-abbey.s: Jumièges Abbey is a ruined Benedictine abbey on a loop of the Seine in Normandy, founded in the 7th century by Saint Philibert. Destroyed by the Vikings and restored by the dukes of Normandy in the 10th century, it became a major monastery whose abbey church was consecrated in…

jesenik.s: Jeseník (German: Freiwaldau) is a town in the Olomouc Region of the Czech Republic, in the Jeseníky mountains near the Polish border. It belonged to the episcopal Duchy of Nysa and remained with Austria when Prussia took most of the duchy in 1742.

jindrich-zdik.s: Jindřich Zdík (c. 1083–1150) was Bishop of Olomouc from 1126 and a leading churchman of 12th-century Bohemia.

jasna-gora-monastery.s: Jasna Góra is a Pauline monastery on a hill in Częstochowa, southern Poland, founded in 1382 by Duke Władysław II of Opole, who brought monks from Hungary. It houses the icon of the Black Madonna.

jan-iv-of-oswiecim.s: Jan IV (d. 1497) was a Piast duke of Oświęcim, from a branch of the dukes of Cieszyn.

justus-perthes.s: Justus Perthes was a publishing house founded in Gotha in 1785 by Johann Georg Justus Perthes. It published the Almanach de Gotha, the standard directory of Europe's royal and noble houses, as well as Stieler's Hand-Atlas and, from 1855, the geographical journal Petermanns…

johannes-brahms.s: Johannes Brahms was a German composer and pianist, born in Hamburg, who settled in Vienna in 1862. Working within classical forms, he wrote four symphonies, concertos, chamber music, songs and A German Requiem, and was seen as the leading heir of Beethoven.

jena.s: Jena is a university city on the Saale river in Thuringia, Germany. Its university, founded in 1558, made it a centre of German philosophy and literature around 1800.

janusz-radziwill-1579-1620.s: Janusz Radziwiłł was a Lithuanian magnate of the Calvinist branch of the Radziwiłł family. In 1600 he married Sophia Olelkovich, heiress of Slutsk, bringing the duchy to the Radziwiłłs.

jozef-poniatowski.s: Józef Poniatowski was a Polish prince and general, nephew of King Stanisław August. He fought against Russia in 1792 and in the Kościuszko Uprising, and from 1807 commanded the army of the Duchy of Warsaw.

jhajjar.s: Jhajjar is a town in Haryana, India, west of Delhi, and the headquarters of Jhajjar district. It was the seat of the Nawabs of Jhajjar until 1857, when the last nawab was executed by the British for supporting the rebellion and his state was confiscated.

jovan-vladimir.s: Jovan Vladimir was ruler of Duklja from around 1000 to 1016. He was defeated by Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria, whose daughter he married, and he ruled as his vassal.

jibal.s: Jibal ("the mountains") was the name used by medieval Arab geographers for the mountainous region of western Iran, roughly ancient Media. Its main cities included Hamadan, Rayy, Isfahan and Qom.

jakarta.s: Jakarta is the largest city of Indonesia, on the north-west coast of Java. Its port, Sunda Kelapa, was taken by Fatahillah in 1527 and renamed Jayakarta.

johannes-vermeer.s: Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch painter who worked in Delft. He painted slowly, and only about 35 works are attributed to him, mostly quiet domestic interiors lit by daylight, such as The Milkmaid and Girl with a Pearl Earring, as well as the townscape View of Delft.

jean-ii-destrees.s: Jean II d'Estrées was a French admiral and Marshal of France. In the Franco-Dutch War he led French fleets in the Caribbean, attacking the Dutch on Tobago in 1677, when an explosion destroyed the Dutch fort.

johan-gustaf-renat.s: Johan Gustaf Renat was a Swedish artillery officer captured by the Russians at Poltava in 1709 and taken to Siberia. Captured again by the Dzungars in 1716, he spent nearly twenty years among them, teaching them to cast cannon and to manufacture other goods.

jacobitism.s: Jacobitism was the movement to restore the Catholic king James II of England and his Stuart descendants to the thrones of England, Scotland and Ireland after his overthrow in 1688. Its supporters, the Jacobites, fought the Williamite war in Ireland and rose in Scotland in…

james-butler-1st-duke-of-ormonde.s: James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormonde, was an Irish nobleman who led the royalist side in Ireland in the wars of the 1640s and went into exile after Cromwell's conquest. He served as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland under both Charles I and Charles II, and was made a duke in 1661 after…

jiao-province.s: Jiao Province, or Jiaozhou, was a province of the Chinese empire covering northern Vietnam and, at times, parts of southern China, under dynasties from the Han to the Tang. Its centre lay in the Red River delta.

jagannath.s: Jagannath, Lord of the Universe, is a Hindu deity worshipped as a form of Vishnu or Krishna, chiefly at his temple in Puri, Odisha, together with Balabhadra and Subhadra. The present temple was begun by the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga in the 12th century, and…

jiankang.s: Jiankang was the capital of the southern Chinese dynasties on the site of modern Nanjing. Founded as Jianye, capital of Sun Quan's state of Eastern Wu from 229, it was renamed Jiankang in 313 and served as the seat of the Eastern Jin and of the Liu Song, Southern Qi, Liang and…

jinyang.s: Jinyang was an ancient city near modern Taiyuan in Shanxi, northern China. Once the base of the Zhao clan of the State of Jin, it later became a key military centre: Gao Huan controlled the Eastern Wei from it, and the Northern Qi treated it as a second capital.

john-berkeley-1st-baron-berkeley-of-stra.n: John Berkeley, 1st Baron Berkeley of Stratton
john-berkeley-1st-baron-berkeley-of-stra.s: John Berkeley, 1st Baron Berkeley of Stratton, was an English Royalist commander and courtier. After serving Charles I in the Civil War and the exiled royal court, he and Sir George Carteret received the proprietorship of New Jersey from the Duke of York in 1664.

jucar.s: The Júcar (Xúquer in Valencian) is a river of eastern Spain, about 500 kilometres long, rising in the Montes Universales and flowing through the province of Cuenca and across the Valencian plain to the Mediterranean at Cullera. Known in antiquity as the Sucro, it marked the…

jbala.s: Jbala is a mountainous region of north-western Morocco, between Tangier, Tetouan and the Rif, and the name of the Arabic-speaking people who live there. Its hills, with towns such as Chefchaouen, were long largely independent of the sultans and were a centre of resistance to…

julamerk.s: Julamerk, in Kurdish Colemêrg, is the historic name of the town of Hakkâri in the mountains of south-eastern Turkey, above the Great Zab valley. It was the seat of the Kurdish emirs of Hakkari from the late Middle Ages until the Ottomans abolished the emirate in the 1840s.

john-kourkouas.s: John Kourkouas was a Byzantine general of Armenian descent who served as domestic of the Schools for more than twenty years under Romanos I Lekapenos. He led the offensive against the Arab emirates of the eastern frontier, capturing Melitene in 934, and in 944 obtained the…

jalam-ibn-shayban.s: Jalam ibn Shayban was an Ismaili missionary who established rule over Multan, in present-day Pakistan, in the second half of the 10th century, recognising the Fatimid caliphs of Egypt. He had the city's famous Sun temple destroyed and a mosque built on its site.

john-glubb.s: John Glubb, known as Glubb Pasha, was a British officer who commanded the Arab Legion of Transjordan and then Jordan from 1939 to 1956. He recruited Bedouin into the desert patrol and made the Legion the most effective Arab army in the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.

juno-curitis.s: Juno Curitis was a form of the goddess Juno worshipped at Falerii, the chief town of the Falisci, and also venerated at Rome. Her festival at Falerii, with its procession of white heifers, young people and priestesses, was described by the poet Ovid, whose wife came from the…

james-hutton-brew.s: James Hutton Brew was a Gold Coast lawyer and journalist of Fante and British descent. He was one of the Western-educated leaders of the Fante Confederacy in the early 1870s and helped draft its constitution.

jose-maria-orellana.s: José María Orellana was a Guatemalan general who came to power in a coup in December 1921 and was then elected president of Guatemala, serving until his death in 1926. Soon after taking office he withdrew Guatemala from the short-lived Federation of Central America.

juan-odonoju.s: Juan O'Donojú was a Spanish general of Irish descent and the last viceroy of New Spain, appointed by the liberal government in Madrid. Arriving in Mexico in 1821 to find the country almost entirely in the hands of Agustín de Iturbide's Army of the Three Guarantees, he signed…

jatila-parantaka-nedunjadaiyan.s: Jatila Parantaka Nedunjadaiyan was a king of the Pandya dynasty of Madurai in the late 8th and early 9th centuries, often identified with Varaguna I. He extended Pandya power over much of the Tamil country, fighting the Pallavas and the chiefs of the Kongu region.

janio-quadros.s: Jânio Quadros was a Brazilian politician who rose rapidly from mayor to governor of São Paulo campaigning against corruption, with a broom as his symbol. He won the presidential election of 1960 by a large margin, but after an erratic seven months in office, marked by an…

jean-de-lery.s: Jean de Léry was a French Protestant pastor and writer who was one of the Calvinists sent from Geneva to the colony of France Antarctique in the bay of Rio de Janeiro in 1557. After quarrelling with the governor Villegaignon, he lived for some months among the Tupinambá.

jorge-tadeo-lozano.s: Jorge Tadeo Lozano was a New Granadan naturalist and politician who became the first president of the Free and Independent State of Cundinamarca in 1811. A member of the Bogotá elite, he headed a constitutional monarchy that still acknowledged Ferdinand VII, but was soon…

jean-rapp.s: Jean Rapp was an Alsatian general of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars and one of Napoleon's aides-de-camp. Governor of Danzig from 1807, he defended the city through a long siege in 1813 before surrendering at the end of the year.

jagiellonian-university.s: The Jagiellonian University in Kraków is the oldest university in Poland, founded by King Casimir III the Great in 1364 and refounded by Władysław II Jagiełło and Queen Jadwiga's bequest in 1400. Nicolaus Copernicus studied there in the 1490s.

johann-smidt.s: Johann Smidt was a Bremen theologian and statesman who served many terms as the city's mayor between 1821 and 1857. He represented Bremen at the Congress of Vienna, helping to secure its independence as a free city in the German Confederation.

johann-lachmann.s: Johann Lachmann was a Lutheran reformer who, as preacher in the imperial city of Heilbronn, led its turn to the Reformation, completed in 1528. He drew on the ideas of Martin Luther and worked closely with Johannes Brenz of nearby Schwäbisch Hall.

jablonec-nad-nisou.s: Jablonec nad Nisou, in German Gablonz an der Neisse, is a town in northern Bohemia, Czech Republic, famous since the 18th century for glass jewellery and costume ornaments. Its largely German population was expelled after the Second World War, and many of the refugees…

johann-geiler-von-kaysersberg.s: Johann Geiler von Kaysersberg was a priest and the most celebrated preacher of late medieval Germany, who held the pulpit of Strasbourg Cathedral from 1478 until his death. Raised in Kaysersberg in Alsace, from which he took his name, he attacked clerical abuses and the vices…

johann-tserclaes-count-of-tilly.s: Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, was a Walloon general who commanded the army of the Catholic League in the Thirty Years' War. He won victories at the White Mountain in 1620, Wimpfen in 1622 and Lutter in 1626, and his army's sack of Magdeburg in 1631 became notorious.

johannes-brenz.s: Johannes Brenz was a Lutheran reformer and theologian who led the Reformation in the imperial city of Schwäbisch Hall from 1522. He later reorganised the church of the Duchy of Württemberg and wrote a widely used catechism and church ordinances that shaped Lutheranism in…

johannes-sturm.s: Johannes Sturm was a German humanist and educator who founded the Protestant Gymnasium of Strasbourg in 1538 and directed it for more than 40 years. His curriculum, based on classical Latin, eloquence and piety, became a model for Protestant grammar schools across Europe, and…

jorg-zurn.s: Jörg Zürn was a German sculptor of the early Baroque from Waldsee in Upper Swabia. His masterpiece is the carved limewood high altar of St.

johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.s: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a German poet, novelist, dramatist and scientist, the central figure of German literature. Born in Frankfurt, he won fame with The Sorrows of Young Werther in 1774 and from 1775 lived in Weimar, where he served as a minister of Duke Charles…

justin-ahomadegbe-tometin.s: Justin Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin was a Dahomeyan politician, a dentist from Abomey whose support lay in the Fon south-centre. With Hubert Maga and Sourou Migan Apithy he formed the regional rivalry that dominated Dahomey's politics after 1946 and through the coups of the 1960s.

jacques-le-moyne-de-morgues.s: Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues was a French artist and cartographer who accompanied René Goulaine de Laudonnière's Huguenot expedition to Florida in 1564. He escaped the Spanish capture of Fort Caroline in 1565 and later settled in London.

jean-monnet.s: Jean Monnet was a French economist and diplomat regarded as a founder of European integration. After the Second World War he headed France's General Planning Commission, whose Monnet Plan guided reconstruction and modernisation from 1946.

jean-baptiste-le-moyne-de-bienville.s: Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville was a French-Canadian colonial officer, younger brother of Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville. He served several terms as governor of French Louisiana between 1701 and 1743, and in 1718 founded New Orleans, which became the colony's capital in 1722.

john-law.s: John Law was a Scottish economist and financier who became controller-general of finances in France. In 1716 he founded the Banque Générale, later the Banque Royale, which issued paper money, and he headed the Mississippi Company, which controlled trade with Louisiana.

jean-baptiste-kleber.s: Jean-Baptiste Kléber was a French general of the Revolutionary Wars from Strasbourg. He fought in the Vendée and on the Rhine, accompanied Napoleon Bonaparte to Egypt, and was left in command when Bonaparte returned to France in 1799.

jacques-francois-menou.s: Jacques-François de Menou was a French general and nobleman who succeeded Jean-Baptiste Kléber as commander of the French army in Egypt in 1800. He converted to Islam, taking the name Abdallah, and married an Egyptian woman.

jean-louis-ferrand.s: Jean-Louis Ferrand was a French general who governed the former Spanish colony of Santo Domingo after French forces withdrew there from Haiti in 1803–1804. He repelled Jean-Jacques Dessalines' siege of the city in 1805, revived trade and restored slavery.

jules-ferry.s: Jules Ferry was a French republican statesman who twice served as prime minister, in 1880–1881 and 1883–1885. As education minister his laws of 1881–1882 made primary schooling free, compulsory and secular.

jiang-guangnai.s: Jiang Guangnai was a Chinese general from Guangdong, commander of the Nineteenth Route Army, which resisted the Japanese attack on Shanghai in January–March 1932. Transferred to Fujian, he and Cai Tingkai led the Fujian Rebellion of November 1933 against Chiang Kai-shek, which…

javols.s: Javols is a village in Lozère in southern France, on the site of Anderitum, the chief town of the Gabali under Roman rule. Excavations have revealed a forum, baths and other remains of the Roman town.

jogulamba-gadwal-district.s: Jogulamba Gadwal district is a district in the south of Telangana, India, between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, with its headquarters at Gadwal. It was formed in 2016 from part of Mahbubnagar district and is named after the goddess Jogulamba, whose temple at Alampur is…

jayachandra.s: Jayachandra was the last major king of the Gahadavala dynasty, ruling Kannauj and Varanasi from about 1170 to 1194. He held a large kingdom in the middle Ganges plain and was a rival of the Chahamana king Prithviraj Chauhan, a rivalry much elaborated in later bardic legend.

james-fort.s: James Fort is a fort on the coast of Accra, Ghana, built by the English Royal African Company in 1673 on the site of an earlier trading lodge. It stood near the Dutch Fort Crèvecoeur and the Danish Christiansborg, the three posts competing for the trade of the Ga kingdom,…

jabiyah.s: Jabiyah was a site in the Golan region of southern Syria, near Nawa, that served as the main camp and court of the Ghassanid kings. After the Muslim conquest it became the chief military camp of the province, and around 638 the caliph Umar held a conference there to organise…

jacob-baradaeus.s: Jacob Baradaeus was a Syrian bishop who organised the Miaphysite church in opposition to the Council of Chalcedon. Consecrated bishop of Edessa around 542 at the request of the Ghassanid king al-Harith, he travelled across the eastern provinces, often in disguise, ordaining…

jangsu-of-goguryeo.s: Jangsu was king of Goguryeo from 413 to 491, one of the longest reigns in Korean history. The son of Gwanggaeto the Great, he moved the capital from Gungnae to Pyongyang in 427 and kept careful relations with the rival Chinese dynasties of the north and south.

ji-an-jilin.s: Ji'an is a city in Jilin province, China, on the Yalu river facing North Korea. As Gungnae it was the capital of Goguryeo for about four centuries, and its surroundings hold the stele of Gwanggaeto the Great and thousands of Goguryeo tombs, including the stepped stone Tomb of…

jolbon.s: Jolbon was, according to Korean tradition, the first capital of Goguryeo, where Jumong founded the kingdom in 37 BCE. It is usually placed in the Huanren area of Liaoning, China, near the mountain fortress of Wunü Shan, now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

jikji.s: The Jikji is a Korean anthology of Seon (Zen) Buddhist teachings compiled by the monk Baegun and printed with movable metal type at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju in 1377. It is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, some 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.

juan-de-salazar.s: Juan de Salazar de Espinosa was a Spanish conquistador who founded Asunción, the capital of Paraguay, on 15 August 1537 as a fort on the Paraguay river, during the search for the missing explorer Juan de Ayolas. The fort became the centre of Spanish settlement in the Río de la…

jangchub-o.s: Jangchub-Ö was a royal monk of the kingdom of Guge in western Tibet in the 11th century, a kinsman of Yeshe-Ö. Continuing his family's patronage of Buddhism, he sent envoys to invite the Indian teacher Atisha, who came to Guge in 1042 and wrote the Lamp for the Path to…

jai-vilas-palace.s: The Jai Vilas Palace is a palace in Gwalior, India, built in 1874 for Jayajirao Scindia, Maharaja of Gwalior, in a European style mixing Italian, Tuscan and Corinthian elements. Designed by Sir Michael Filose, it is known for its vast durbar hall and huge crystal chandeliers.

jayajirao-scindia.s: Jayajirao Scindia was Maharaja of Gwalior from 1843 to 1886. During the rebellion of 1857 he remained loyal to the British, though much of his army joined the rebels, and in 1858 the Rani of Jhansi and Tatya Tope briefly seized Gwalior fort before British forces retook it.

johann-ludwig-burckhardt.s: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt was a Swiss traveller and orientalist who explored the Near East in the guise of a Muslim scholar, Sheikh Ibrahim. In 1812 he noticed inscribed stones at Hama, later recognised as Hittite hieroglyphs, and became the first European in modern times to…

judas-maccabeus.s: Judas Maccabeus was a Jewish priest and military leader, the third son of Mattathias, who led the revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV from 166 BCE. He recaptured Jerusalem and rededicated the Temple in 164 BCE, an event commemorated by Hanukkah.

judas-of-galilee.s: Judas of Galilee was a Jewish leader who led resistance to the census of Quirinius when Judaea became a Roman province in 6 CE, teaching that paying tax to Rome meant accepting a human master in place of God. Josephus calls his movement a 'fourth philosophy' beside the…

jericho.s: Jericho is a city in the West Bank near the Jordan River, north of the Dead Sea, and one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world, with settlement at Tell es-Sultan from about 9000 BCE. Its springs and palm groves made it a royal estate under the Hasmoneans and…

jayapala.s: Jayapala was a king of the Hindu Shahi dynasty in the late 10th century, ruling from the Kabul valley to the Punjab. He lost a series of wars against the Ghaznavid rulers Sabuktigin and Mahmud of Ghazni, who defeated and captured him near Peshawar in 1001.

jiaozhi-province.s: Jiaozhi Province was the Ming Chinese province created in northern Vietnam after the Yongle Emperor's armies overthrew the Hồ dynasty in 1407, reviving an old Han-era name. Ming rule brought heavy taxation and efforts at cultural assimilation and provoked repeated revolts.

jauja.s: Jauja is a town in the Junín region of central Peru, in the Mantaro valley. Near the Inca centre of Hatun Xauxa, it was founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1534 as the first Spanish capital of Peru, a role soon passed to Lima in 1535.

jingkou.s: Jingkou was the ancient name of Zhenjiang, a city on the south bank of the Yangtze in Jiangsu, China, at its junction with the Grand Canal. Under the Eastern Jin it was a major military base and home to many northern refugee families, and it was the headquarters of the Beifu…

jozsef-antall.s: József Antall was a Hungarian historian and politician who became the first freely elected prime minister of Hungary after communism, in 1990. As leader of the Hungarian Democratic Forum he headed a centre-right coalition that began the transition to a market economy and…

jaca.s: Jaca is a town in the province of Huesca, Aragon, Spain, in the upper valley of the Aragón river near the Pyrenees. As Iaca it was a town of the Iacetani and later a Roman settlement.

jacques-marquette.s: Jacques Marquette was a French Jesuit missionary in New France. In 1673 he and the explorer Louis Jolliet travelled from the Great Lakes down the Mississippi as far as the mouth of the Arkansas river, becoming the first Europeans to map much of its course.

joseph-gabler.s: Joseph Gabler was a German organ builder from Ochsenhausen in upper Swabia. After building an organ for the abbey church of his home town, he created his most famous instrument, the great organ of Weingarten Abbey, completed in 1750 with more than 6,000 pipes.

jasenovac-concentration-camp.s: Jasenovac was the largest concentration and extermination camp of the Independent State of Croatia, run by the Ustaše regime from 1941 to 1945 on the Sava River. Tens of thousands of Serbs, Jews, Roma and Croatian anti-fascists were murdered there, many by brutal methods.

jones-law-philippines.s: The Jones Law, or Philippine Autonomy Act, was a United States law of 1916 that replaced the Philippine Commission with an elected Philippine Senate, creating an all-Filipino legislature. Its preamble stated that the United States would grant independence once a stable…

jones-shafroth-act.s: The Jones–Shafroth Act was a United States law of 1917 that granted United States citizenship to the people of Puerto Rico. It also reorganised the island's government, creating an elected Senate and a bill of rights, while the governor and other high officials were still…

jamiat-e-islami.s: Jamiat-e Islami is an Afghan Islamist party led for decades by Burhanuddin Rabbani, with mainly Tajik support in the north and north-east. Its commanders, notably Ahmad Shah Massoud, were among the most effective mujahideen against the Soviet Union.

jubaland.s: Jubaland is a region of southern Somalia west of the Jubba River, centred on the port of Kismayo. Britain ceded it from Kenya Colony to Italy in 1924 as a reward for Italy's part in the First World War, and it was joined to Italian Somaliland in 1926.

jaffna.s: Jaffna is the main city of northern Sri Lanka, on the Jaffna peninsula, and the cultural centre of the Sri Lankan Tamils. From the 13th century it was the seat of the Jaffna kingdom, and after 1619 a Portuguese and then Dutch stronghold, with a large Dutch fort.

jantar-mantar.s: Jantar Mantar is the name of the five astronomical observatories built by Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber in the 1720s and 1730s at Jaipur, Delhi, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura. They consist of huge masonry instruments for measuring time and the positions of celestial bodies.

jalairs.s: The Jalairs were a Mongol tribe that served Genghis Khan and his successors; his general Muqali was a Jalair. Jalair commanders were prominent in the Ilkhanate of Iran, and after its collapse one of them, Hasan Buzurg, founded the Jalayirid dynasty in Iraq in the 1330s.

junayd-painter.s: Junayd was a Persian manuscript painter working in Baghdad for the Jalayirid sultan Ahmad Jalayir in the late 14th century. His signed illustrations to a copy of the poems of Khwaju Kirmani, dated 1396 and now in the British Library, are among the earliest signed Persian…

jambughoda-wildlife-sanctuary.s: Jambughoda Wildlife Sanctuary is a protected area of dry deciduous forest and hills in the Panchmahal district of eastern Gujarat, India. It covers lands of the former princely state of Jambughoda, near the historic sites of Champaner and Pavagadh, and shelters leopards, sloth…

jama-masjid-jaunpur.s: The Jama Masjid of Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh, is the largest mosque built by the Sharqi sultans of Jaunpur. Begun in the 1430s and completed around 1470 under Husain Shah Sharqi, it stands on a raised platform and has a towering arched gateway screen before its domed prayer hall,…

jaunpur.s: Jaunpur is a city on the Gomti river in eastern Uttar Pradesh, India, founded in the 14th century by the Delhi sultan Firuz Shah Tughluq. From 1394 to 1479 it was the capital of the Sharqi sultans, whose patronage of scholars earned it the name Shiraz of India.

jhalrapatan.s: Jhalrapatan is a town in the Jhalawar district of south-eastern Rajasthan, India, beside the later capital of Jhalawar State. Known as the city of temple bells, it has many old temples, of which the 10th-century Sun Temple is the most famous.
