johor-bahru.s: Johor Bahru is the capital of the Malaysian state of Johor, at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula across the strait from Singapore. Founded in 1855 as Tanjung Puteri by the Temenggong Daeng Ibrahim, it was renamed and made the capital by his son Abu Bakar in the 1860s.

johor-lama.s: Johor Lama, Old Johor, is a historic site on the Johor River in southern Malaysia that served as the capital of the Johor Sultanate in the 16th century. The successors of the sultans of Malacca built a fortified town there, which Aceh and the Portuguese attacked repeatedly;…

jeongjo-of-joseon.s: Jeongjo was the 22nd king of Joseon Korea, ruling from 1776 to 1800. The son of the executed Crown Prince Sado, he continued his grandfather Yeongjo's policy of balancing court factions, founded the royal library Kyujanggak to promote scholarship and built the Hwaseong…

jiaohe-ruins.s: The Jiaohe Ruins are the remains of an ancient city near Turpan in Xinjiang, China, on a narrow island plateau between two river channels. The capital of the Jushi kingdom, it later became a Chinese garrison and was the first seat of the Tang Protectorate General of Anxi from…

jainism.s: Jainism is an Indian religion that teaches liberation of the soul through non-violence, truthfulness, non-attachment and strict self-discipline. Its followers revere 24 tirthankaras, the last of whom, Mahavira, lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE.

jayakeshi-i.s: Jayakeshi I was a king of the Kadamba dynasty of Goa in the 11th century, ruling as a feudatory of the Western Chalukya Empire. He moved the Kadamba capital from Chandrapura to the port of Gopakapattana on the Zuari river, which grew into a busy harbour trading with Arabia,…

jodo-shinshu.s: Jōdo Shinshū, the True Pure Land school, is a school of Japanese Buddhism founded by Shinran in the 13th century, teaching salvation through faith in the Buddha Amida. Revived by Rennyo in the 15th century, its Hongan-ji organisation won mass support among farmers and…

jaghjagh-river.s: The Jaghjagh River is a tributary of the Khabur that rises in the Tur Abdin hills of south-eastern Turkey and flows south past Nusaybin and Qamishli into north-eastern Syria. Known in antiquity as the Mygdonius, it watered one of the most densely settled parts of ancient Upper…

jameh-mosque-of-isfahan.s: The Jameh Mosque of Isfahan is the great congregational mosque of Isfahan in central Iran, rebuilt and extended continuously from the 8th to the 17th century. Its Seljuk domes of the 1080s and its four-iwan courtyard plan made it a model for later Iranian mosques, and earlier…

jajalladeva-i.s: Jajalladeva I was a king of the Kalachuris of Ratanpur in Dakshina Kosala, modern Chhattisgarh, in the late 11th and early 12th centuries. He threw off the authority of the parent Kalachuri line of Tripuri and extended his kingdom against neighbouring powers.

jabalpur.s: Jabalpur is a city on the Narmada river in Madhya Pradesh, central India. Nearby Tewar was the site of Tripuri, the capital of the Kalachuris, and later the region formed the heart of the Gond kingdom of Garha.

junagarh-fort.s: Junagarh Fort is a fort in the city of Bikaner in Rajasthan, India, built between 1589 and 1594 by Karan Chand, minister of Raja Rai Singh, a general of the Mughal emperor Akbar. Unlike most Rajput forts it stands on the plain rather than a hill.

jepara.s: Jepara is a port town on the north coast of Central Java, Indonesia. In the 16th century it was the seat of Ratu Kalinyamat, who sent fleets against Portuguese Malacca, and Portuguese writers called her the queen of Japara.

jokyu-war.s: The Jōkyū War of 1221 was a brief conflict in which the retired emperor Go-Toba tried to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate. The Hojo regent Hojo Yoshitoki sent armies that took Kyoto within weeks.

jagatjit-palace.s: The Jagatjit Palace is a palace in Kapurthala, Punjab, India, built between 1900 and 1908 for Maharaja Jagatjit Singh of Kapurthala. Modelled on the Palace of Versailles, with French-style gardens and interiors, it reflected the ruler's admiration for France.

jadaun.s: The Jadaun are a Rajput clan of northern India who claim descent from the Yadavas, the lineage of Krishna. In the early medieval period they ruled the region of Bayana in eastern Rajasthan, and a branch later founded the state of Karauli, which its Jadaun Maharajas ruled until…

jayapida.s: Jayapida was a king of Kashmir of the Karkota dynasty in the late 8th century, a grandson of Lalitaditya Muktapida. According to Kalhana's Rajatarangini he campaigned in northern India and was a generous patron of learning, with the grammarians and critics Vamana and Udbhata…

jyotirishvara-thakur.s: Jyotirishvara Thakur was a Maithili poet and scholar at the court of Harisimhadeva, last king of the Karnat dynasty of Mithila, in the early 14th century. His Varna Ratnakara, an encyclopedic collection of descriptions, is one of the earliest prose works in Maithili and in any…

jageshwar.s: Jageshwar is a temple site in a cedar-forested valley in Almora district of Uttarakhand, India. More than a hundred stone temples, mostly dedicated to Shiva, were built there between about the 7th and 12th centuries, many associated with the Katyuri kings, and the site remains…

joshimath.s: Joshimath is a hill town in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, India, above the confluence of the Alaknanda and Dhauliganga rivers. Tradition holds that Adi Shankaracharya founded one of his four monasteries, Jyotirmath, there, and that it was the first seat of the Katyuri kings.

jayakatwang.s: Jayakatwang was a ruler of Gelang-gelang in East Java and a descendant of the kings of Kediri. In 1292 he rebelled and killed Kertanegara, king of Singhasari, reviving Kediri as the leading power in Java.

juang.s: The Juang are an Adivasi people of the hills of Keonjhar and Dhenkanal in Odisha, India, who speak a Munda language. They long practised shifting cultivation and gathering in the forests, and are now classed as a particularly vulnerable tribal group.

janid-dynasty.s: The Janids, also called Ashtarkhanids, were a Chinggisid dynasty that ruled the Khanate of Bukhara from 1599 to 1785. Descended from the khans of Astrakhan, they succeeded the Shaybanids, to whom they were linked by marriage.

jama-masjid-burhanpur.s: The Jama Masjid of Burhanpur is the congregational mosque of Burhanpur in Madhya Pradesh, India, completed in 1590 under Raja Ali Khan, the Faruqi sultan of Khandesh also known as Adil Shah IV. Built of black stone with two tall minarets, it carries inscriptions in Arabic and…

jiaozhou-bay.s: Jiaozhou Bay is an inlet of the Yellow Sea on the southern coast of the Shandong peninsula in eastern China, with the city of Qingdao on its eastern side. Germany occupied it in 1897 and leased it from the Qing in 1898 as the Kiautschou Bay concession, which Japan captured in…

john-lander.s: John Lander was a Cornish explorer who, with his elder brother Richard Lander, traced the lower course of the Niger to its mouth in 1830, settling the long-standing European question of where the river reached the sea. On the way they were captured on the lower Niger and held…

justicia-de-aragon.s: The Justicia de Aragón was the chief judge of the Kingdom of Aragon, chosen from the knights, who settled disputes between the king and the nobility and guarded the kingdom's fueros. He could take people and property under his protection against royal officials, and in the…

jigme-dorji-wangchuck.s: Jigme Dorji Wangchuck was the third king of Bhutan, reigning from 1952 until his death in 1972. He began the country's modernisation, creating a national assembly in 1953, abolishing serfdom, reforming land ownership and starting planned development with Indian help.

jigawa-state.s: Jigawa State is a state in north-western Nigeria, created from part of Kano State in 1991, with its capital at Dutse. Largely flat savanna crossed by the Hadejia river, it is mainly agricultural.

jajce.s: Jajce is a town in central Bosnia and Herzegovina at the falls where the Pliva meets the Vrbas. Its fortress was a seat of Bosnian kings, and the last king, Stephen Tomašević, was executed there in 1463.

josip-jelacic.s: Josip Jelačić was ban of Croatia from 1848 to 1859 and a general in the Austrian army. In the revolutions of 1848 he led Croatian forces against the Hungarian revolutionary government and helped crush the uprising in Vienna.

josip-juraj-strossmayer.s: Josip Juraj Strossmayer was a Croatian Catholic bishop of Đakovo from 1849, a politician and a patron of learning. A leading advocate of South Slav unity and cultural cooperation, he funded the founding of the Yugoslav Academy of Sciences and Arts in 1866 and supported the…

janus-of-cyprus.s: Janus was king of Cyprus from 1398 to 1432. Born while his father was a prisoner of Genoa, he tried without success to recover Famagusta from the Genoese.

jelling.s: Jelling is a small town in central Jutland, Denmark, and was the royal seat of Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth in the 10th century. Its monuments, two great burial mounds, a stone ship setting, a church and the two Jelling runestones, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

jamgon-kongtrul.s: Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Thayé was a Tibetan Buddhist scholar and teacher from Kham and one of the founders of the non-sectarian Rimé movement. Working with Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo, he gathered teachings from all the Tibetan traditions into vast collections known as the Five…

joel-of-dotawo.s: Joel was a king of Dotawo, the last Christian kingdom of Nubia on the middle Nile, in the later 15th century. He is known from documents and inscriptions from Gebel Adda and Qasr Ibrim, the latest dated to 1484, which make him the last securely attested king of Christian Nubia.

john-bates-thurston.s: Sir John Bates Thurston was a British colonial official who served as a minister in Cakobau's Kingdom of Fiji before the cession of 1874. He then rose in the British colonial service to become governor of Fiji and High Commissioner for the Western Pacific from 1888 until his…

jehu.s: Jehu was king of Israel from about 841 to 814 BCE. An army commander, he seized the throne in a bloody coup supported by the prophet Elisha, killing King Joram of Israel, King Ahaziah of Judah and Queen Jezebel and wiping out the house of Omri.

jaffa.s: Jaffa is an ancient port on the Mediterranean coast of Israel, now part of Tel Aviv–Yafo. Long the main sea gateway to Jerusalem, it was taken by the crusaders in 1099 and became the centre of the County of Jaffa and Ascalon.

jeremiah.s: Jeremiah was a Hebrew prophet in Jerusalem from the late 7th century BCE until after its destruction by the Babylonians in 587 BCE. He warned that Judah would fall for its unfaithfulness and urged submission to Babylon, which led to his imprisonment under King Zedekiah.

josiah.s: Josiah was king of Judah from about 640 to 609 BCE. According to the Bible, the discovery of a 'book of the law' in the Temple during his reign led him to carry out a sweeping religious reform, abolishing other cults and centralising worship in Jerusalem.

john-hanning-speke.s: John Hanning Speke was a British army officer and explorer of East Africa. On Richard Burton's expedition he reached Lake Victoria in 1858 and identified it as the source of the Nile, a claim he set out to prove with James Augustus Grant in 1860–63, travelling through Karagwe…

jola.s: The Jola, or Diola, are a West African people of the lower Casamance in Senegal, The Gambia and northern Guinea-Bissau. Known for wet-rice farming in the coastal swamps and for village societies without centralised kingship, they remained largely independent until the colonial…

jataka-tales.s: The Jataka tales are a large body of stories about the previous births of the Buddha, in which he appears as a human or an animal practising the virtues that lead to enlightenment. The Pali collection of the Theravada canon contains 547 tales, many set in Varanasi under kings…

jutes.s: The Jutes were a Germanic people who, according to Bede, came from Jutland and settled in Kent, the Isle of Wight and parts of Hampshire in the 5th century, alongside the Angles and Saxons. Kent's royal house traced its origin to the Jutish leaders Hengist and Horsa.

jutland.s: Jutland is the peninsula of northern Europe that forms the mainland of Denmark, together with the northern part of the German state of Schleswig-Holstein. Probably the homeland of the Jutes and Angles who migrated to Britain in the 5th century, it was a core land of the early…

juka-sambala.s: Juka Sambala was king of Khasso on the upper Senegal River in the mid-19th century. An ally of the French, he supported Governor Louis Faidherbe in building a fort at Médine in 1855, and in 1857 he and the fort's commander Paul Holle held out against a siege by the army of El…

jetavana.s: Jetavana was a monastery in a grove outside Shravasti, the capital of Kosala, given to the Buddha by the merchant Anathapindika. The Buddha is said to have spent 19 rainy seasons there, more than anywhere else, and many of his discourses are set in it.

jiangling.s: Jiangling is an ancient city on the north bank of the Yangtze in Hubei, China, now part of Jingzhou. Close to the old Chu capital of Ying, it was the seat of Nan commandery under the Qin and Han, the capital of the Liang dynasty under Emperor Yuan until Western Wei sacked it…

joseph-radetzky-von-radetz.s: Joseph Radetzky von Radetz was an Austrian field marshal of Bohemian birth who served as chief of staff in the campaigns of 1813–1814 against Napoleon. Commanding in Lombardy-Venetia, he withdrew from Milan in the revolution of 1848, defeated Piedmont-Sardinia at Custoza in…

james-iii-of-scotland.s: James III was king of Scots from 1460 to 1488, succeeding as a child after his father James II was killed at the siege of Roxburgh. His marriage to Margaret of Denmark brought Orkney and Shetland to the Scottish crown in pledge for her dowry in 1468–1469, and they were annexed…

javier-de-burgos.s: Javier de Burgos was a Spanish politician, writer and translator from Motril. As minister of development in 1833 he carried out the territorial division of Spain into 49 provinces grouped in historical regions, which with few changes remains the basis of Spanish provinces today.

jampa-lhakhang.s: Jampa Lhakhang is a 15th-century Buddhist temple in Lo Manthang, the walled capital of the former Kingdom of Lo in Mustang, Nepal. Dedicated to Maitreya, whose large statue fills its central hall, it is decorated with mandala murals of exceptional quality.

jimenez-dynasty.s: The Jiménez dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Pamplona, later Navarre, from 905, when Sancho Garcés I took the throne, until 1234. Its greatest king, Sancho III, dominated Christian Spain in the early 11th century, and his sons founded the royal lines of Castile and Aragon.

jimena-diaz.s: Jimena Díaz was the wife of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, El Cid, and a relative of King Alfonso VI of León and Castile. After the Cid's death in 1099 she governed Valencia and defended it against the Almoravids until 1102, when Alfonso evacuated the city and burned it.

jalisco.s: Jalisco is a state of western Mexico, with its capital at Guadalajara, the country's second-largest city. Its lands formed the core of the colonial kingdom of New Galicia, conquered by Nuño de Guzmán from 1529, and later the intendancy of Guadalajara.

juffure.s: Juffure is a village on the north bank of the Gambia River in The Gambia, close to Albreda. It became world famous after Alex Haley's book Roots (1976) identified it as the home of his ancestor Kunta Kinteh, who was enslaved in the 18th century.

jarnac-convention.s: The Jarnac Convention was an agreement signed by Britain and France on 19 June 1847 in which both powers recognised the independence of the Leeward Islands of the Society group, Huahine, Raiatea and Bora Bora, and agreed not to annex them. It followed the Franco-Tahitian War,…

john-williams-missionary.s: John Williams was an English Congregationalist missionary of the London Missionary Society who worked in the South Pacific from 1817. Based on Raiatea, he spread Christianity through the Society, Cook and Samoan islands using Polynesian teachers, and visited Rarotonga in 1823…

jarawa-berbers.s: The Jarawa were a Zenata Berber tribe of the Aurès mountains in present-day Algeria in the 7th century. Under their leader Dihya, called al-Kahina, they led Berber resistance to the Umayyad conquest of North Africa in the 690s.

johan-rudolf-thorbecke.s: Johan Rudolf Thorbecke was a Dutch liberal statesman and professor of law. He led the drafting of the constitutional revision of 1848, which introduced ministerial responsibility, direct elections to the Second Chamber and basic civil freedoms, establishing parliamentary…

joao-dos-santos.s: João dos Santos was a Portuguese Dominican friar who served as a missionary at Sofala and along the Zambezi in Mozambique in the late 16th century. His book Ethiopia Oriental, published at Évora in 1609, describes the peoples, kingdoms and customs of south-east Africa,…

joanot-martorell.s: Joanot Martorell was a Valencian knight and writer of the 15th century, the main author of the chivalric romance Tirant lo Blanc. Written in Catalan and published at Valencia in 1490, after his death, the book follows a Breton knight who saves the Byzantine Empire.

juan-de-ampies.s: Juan de Ampíes was a Spanish royal official at Santo Domingo who was entrusted with the coast of Venezuela and the nearby islands of Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire. In 1527 he founded the town of Coro on the Venezuelan coast, seeking to deal peacefully with the local Caquetío people.

juan-de-carvajal.s: Juan de Carvajal was a Spanish conquistador who governed Venezuela as acting governor in the 1540s, after the Welser company's authority weakened. In 1545 he founded El Tocuyo in the interior.

japan-korea-treaty-of-1905.s: The Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905, known in Korea as the Eulsa Treaty, was signed on 17 November 1905 after the Russo-Japanese War. Pushed through by Itō Hirobumi with troops surrounding the palace and without the emperor's signature, it took control of Korea's foreign relations…

jan-vansina.s: Jan Vansina was a Belgian historian and anthropologist who pioneered the use of oral tradition as a source for African history. His fieldwork among the Kuba of the Congo and in Rwanda in the 1950s led to studies such as Oral Tradition (1961) and The Children of Woot, a history…

jin-shuren.s: Jin Shuren was a Chinese official who governed Xinjiang from 1928, after the assassination of Yang Zengxin, until 1933. His abolition of the Kumul Khanate in 1930, heavy taxes and settlement of Han Chinese provoked the Kumul Rebellion, which spread across the province and drew…

jukun-people.s: The Jukun are a people of the middle Benue valley in north-eastern Nigeria, living mainly in Taraba and neighbouring states. They are identified with the power called Kwararafa in Hausa and Bornu sources, which raided Kano and other Hausa cities in the 17th century.

jalal-abad.s: Jalal-Abad is a city in southern Kyrgyzstan, on the edge of the Fergana Valley near the Uzbek border, and the capital of Jalal-Abad Region. Known for its mineral springs, it is with Osh one of the main centres of the south, where Kyrgyz and Uzbek communities live side by side.

john-hawley-glover.s: John Hawley Glover was a Royal Navy officer and colonial administrator who served as administrator of the British colony of Lagos for most of the years from 1863 to 1872. He extended British influence into the Yoruba hinterland and raised an armed Hausa police force, the…

james-erskine-murray.s: James Erskine Murray was a Scottish adventurer who in 1843 sailed to Borneo hoping, like James Brooke in Sarawak, to win a territory of his own. His attempt to gain trading concessions from the Sultan of Kutai on the Mahakam River ended in fighting in early 1844, in which he…

janamejaya.s: Janamejaya was a Kuru king of the late Vedic period, son of Parikshit, remembered in the Brahmanas as a performer of the horse sacrifice. Under him and his father the Kuru realm became the leading power of northern India.

johann-gottfried-herder.s: Johann Gottfried Herder was a German philosopher, theologian and writer, born in Mohrungen in East Prussia. A leading figure of the Sturm und Drang and of Weimar Classicism, he argued that each people has its own language, culture and character, and he collected folk songs…

jeonju.s: Jeonju is the capital of North Jeolla province in south-western South Korea. Known as Wansanju in the Unified Silla period, it became the capital of Later Baekje when Gyeon Hwon proclaimed himself king there in 900.

jatavarman-sundara-pandya-i.s: Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I was the most powerful king of the Later Pandya dynasty of south India. He defeated the Cholas and the Hoysalas, campaigned in Sri Lanka and extended Pandya rule north to Nellore, where he performed a victory coronation.

joseph-aoun.s: Joseph Aoun is a Lebanese army general and politician who became president of Lebanon in January 2025. He was commander of the Lebanese Armed Forces from 2017, leading the army through the financial collapse of 2019 and the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah.

juba-i.s: Juba I was king of Numidia from about 60 to 46 BCE. In Caesar's civil war he sided with the Pompeians, destroying the army of Caesar's legate Curio on the Bagradas river in 49 BCE, but after the Pompeian defeat at Thapsus in 46 BCE he took his own life.

jugurtha.s: Jugurtha was king of Numidia, a grandson of Masinissa who seized the whole kingdom after killing one adoptive brother and fighting the other. His massacre of Italian traders at Cirta in 112 BCE led to the Jugurthine War with Rome, which exposed corruption in the Roman Senate.

jhalawad.s: Jhalawad was one of the historic regions, or prants, of Kathiawar in Gujarat, western India, in the north-east of the peninsula near the Little Rann of Kutch. It took its name from the Jhala Rajputs, who ruled several of its princely states, including Dhrangadhra, Limbdi and…

julius-sabinus.s: Julius Sabinus was a nobleman of the Lingones in Gaul who, during the revolt of the Batavi in 69–70 CE, proclaimed himself Caesar and led his people against Rome. Defeated by the Sequani, he spread word of his death and hid with his wife Epponina in an underground refuge for…

jayasimha-of-kashmir.s: Jayasimha was a king of Kashmir of the second Lohara dynasty, reigning from 1128 to 1155. He restored some stability after decades of civil war by balancing and buying off the powerful Damara landholders.

juntas-generales-of-biscay.s: The Juntas Generales of Biscay are the general assembly of the province of Biscay in the Basque Country. In the Middle Ages they met under the oak of Guernica, where the lords of Biscay swore to respect the fueros, and they governed the province's affairs until the fueros were…

james-hamilton-1st-viscount-claneboye.s: James Hamilton, 1st Viscount Claneboye, was a Scottish schoolmaster turned agent of James VI who, with Hugh Montgomery, acquired much of Con O'Neill's lordship of Clandeboye in north Down in 1605. Their private settlement brought many Scottish colonists to Ulster before the…

john-balliol.s: John Balliol was king of Scotland from 1292 to 1296, chosen by Edward I of England from among the claimants after the death of Margaret, Maid of Norway. A descendant of David I and, through his mother Dervorguilla, of the lords of Galloway, he was humiliated by Edward's…

jever.s: Jever is a town in Friesland in north-western Germany, known for its castle and its brewery. It was the centre of the Frisian land of Östringen and later of the Lordship of Jever, ruled by local chieftains and in the 16th century by Lady Mary of Jever.

james-stanley-7th-earl-of-derby.s: James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby, was an English royalist commander and Lord of Mann. During the English Civil War he fought for Charles I and used the Isle of Man as a royalist base.

john-stanley-died-1414.s: Sir John Stanley was an English soldier and royal servant who founded the fortunes of the Stanley family. He served as lieutenant of Ireland under Richard II and Henry IV, and in 1405 Henry IV granted him the Isle of Man, which his descendants held as Kings and then Lords of…

james-iv-of-scotland.s: James IV was King of Scotland from 1488 to 1513, a Renaissance ruler who strengthened royal authority, built a navy and patronised learning and printing. He forfeited the Lordship of the Isles in 1493 and married Margaret Tudor in 1503.

john-of-islay-earl-of-ross.n: John of Islay, Earl of Ross
john-of-islay-earl-of-ross.s: John of Islay, also called John MacDonald II, was the last Lord of the Isles and Earl of Ross. In 1462 he made the secret Treaty of Westminster-Ardtornish with Edward IV of England to partition Scotland.

joao-maria-ferreira-do-amaral.s: João Maria Ferreira do Amaral was a Portuguese naval officer and governor of Macau from 1846 to 1849. He imposed taxes on the Chinese population, expelled the Chinese customs officials and stopped paying ground rent to China, turning Macau into a fully Portuguese colony.

jeolla-province.s: Jeolla Province was one of the Eight Provinces of Joseon Korea, in the fertile south-west of the peninsula, divided in 1896 into North and South Jeolla. Once part of the Mahan confederacy and then Baekje, it was the base of Later Baekje in the 10th century and of the Donghak…

jama-masjid-mandu.s: The Jama Masjid of Mandu is a great mosque begun by Hoshang Shah, sultan of Malwa, and completed by Mahmud Khalji in 1454. Built of red sandstone on a high plinth, with large domes and a vast courtyard, it is said to have been modelled on the Great Mosque of Damascus.

jahaz-mahal.s: The Jahaz Mahal ('ship palace') is a 15th-century palace at Mandu in Madhya Pradesh, India, attributed to the Malwa sultan Ghiyath Shah. Long and narrow, it stands between two artificial lakes, so that it seems to float like a ship.

john-ball.s: John Ball was an English priest whose preaching on the equality of all people made him one of the leaders of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Excommunicated and imprisoned several times for sermons attacking the wealth of the Church and the lords, he was freed from Maidstone…

john-f-kennedy.s: John F. Kennedy was the thirty-fifth president of the United States, serving from 1961 until his assassination in Dallas in November 1963.

jewish-agency-for-israel.s: The Jewish Agency, founded in 1929 as the Jewish Agency for Palestine, was the body recognised under the British mandate to represent the Jewish community in Palestine and advise the authorities. Led from 1935 by David Ben-Gurion, it organised immigration, land settlement and…

joginder-sen.s: Joginder Sen was the last ruling raja of Mandi, a princely state in the western Himalaya, from 1913 until it merged into Himachal Pradesh in 1948. His reign saw the building of the Shanan hydroelectric power station, opened in 1932, one of the earliest in India, and the town…

john-margrave-of-brandenburg-kustrin.s: John, Margrave of Brandenburg-Küstrin, known as Hans of Küstrin, was a younger son of Elector Joachim I of Brandenburg who received the Neumark east of the Oder in 1535. He introduced the Lutheran Reformation in 1538, turned Küstrin into a strong fortress and ran a thrifty,…

jakob-bohme.s: Jakob Böhme was a German Lutheran mystic and philosopher, a shoemaker in Görlitz in Upper Lusatia. His first work, Aurora (1612), describing visions of God and nature, led the town's pastor to have him banned from writing.

jiroft.s: Jiroft is a city in Kerman province in south-eastern Iran, in the Halil river valley. From 2001 looting near the town revealed the Jiroft culture of the 3rd millennium BCE, with large settlements such as Konar Sandal and finely carved chlorite vessels, some of which reached…

jaluit-atoll.s: Jaluit is a coral atoll in the Ralik chain of the Marshall Islands in the central Pacific. German traders based their copra business there, and from 1885 it was the administrative centre of the German Marshall Islands protectorate.

jaluit-gesellschaft.s: The Jaluit Gesellschaft was a German trading company formed in 1887 by Hamburg firms engaged in the copra trade of the Marshall Islands. From 1888 it paid the costs of administering the German protectorate in return for a monopoly of trade and land rights, so the colony was in…

jaipur.s: Jaipur is the capital and largest city of Rajasthan in north-western India. It was founded in 1727 by the Kachhwaha ruler Sawai Jai Singh II as a planned city on a grid, replacing nearby Amber as the capital of his kingdom, and he built the Jantar Mantar observatory there.

jamshedpur.s: Jamshedpur is an industrial city in Jharkhand, eastern India, founded as a company town by the Tata Iron and Steel Company. Named after Jamsetji Tata, who planned India's first large steel works, it grew around the plant at Sakchi, which began production in 1912 using iron ore…

jraberd.s: Jraberd was one of the five Armenian melikdoms of Karabakh, known as the Khamsa, in the valley of the Tartar river in the north of the region. Ruled by the Melik-Israelian family, it took its name from the fortress of Jraberd.

jamukha.s: Jamukha was a Mongol leader of the Jadaran clan and a childhood sworn brother (anda) of Temüjin, later Genghis Khan. He helped Temüjin rescue Börte from the Merkits, but they became rivals, and in 1201 Jamukha was proclaimed gurkhan by a coalition of tribes opposed to Temüjin.

javanshir.s: Javanshir was the most famous prince of Caucasian Albania, of the Mihranid family, ruling from about 637 until 680. After serving the Sasanians against the Arabs, he led Albania on its own course, allying with the Byzantine Empire, fighting off Khazar raids and in 667…

john-i-tzimiskes.s: John I Tzimiskes was Byzantine emperor from 969 to 976, an Armenian-born general who seized the throne by murdering his uncle Nikephoros II Phokas. He defeated the Rus prince Sviatoslav in Bulgaria in 971, annexed eastern Bulgaria and campaigned into Syria and Palestine…

john-j-pershing.s: John J. Pershing was an American army officer who served as military governor of the Moro Province in the southern Philippines from 1909 to 1913, where he disarmed the population and fought the Battle of Bud Bagsak.

joseph-whitaker.s: Joseph Whitaker was an English-Sicilian ornithologist and archaeologist from a family of Marsala wine merchants. He bought the island of San Pantaleo, the site of ancient Motya, and from 1906 carried out the first systematic excavations there, publishing his results in 1921.

john-ii-komnenos.s: John II Komnenos was Byzantine emperor from 1118 to 1143, the son of Alexios I. He fought the Pechenegs, Hungarians and Serbs in the Balkans and recovered lands from the Turks in Anatolia.

jalingo.s: Jalingo is a city in north-eastern Nigeria and the capital of Taraba State, created in 1991. It became the seat of the emirate of Muri in the 1890s, and the Emir of Muri still resides there.

jizan.s: Jizan is a port city on the Red Sea in south-western Saudi Arabia and the capital of Jizan Province. It was part of the Idrisid emirate of Asir in the early 20th century and came under Saudi rule in the 1930s.

jason.s: In Greek mythology, Jason was the hero of Iolkos in Thessaly who led the Argonauts on the ship Argo to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis. His uncle Pelias had taken the throne and sent him on the quest; with the help of the princess Medea he succeeded.

jaito-morcha.s: The Jaito Morcha was a protest campaign by the Akali movement at Jaito in the princely state of Nabha, India, from 1923 to 1925. It began after the British forced Maharaja Ripudaman Singh to abdicate, when volunteers held prayers for him at the Gangsar gurdwara.

jagat-seth.s: Jagat Seth, meaning 'banker of the world', was the hereditary title of a Marwari banking family based at Murshidabad in Bengal, granted by the Mughal emperor in 1723. The family managed the Bengal mint and revenue remittances and lent to nawabs and the East India Company alike.

john-of-austria-the-younger.s: John of Austria the Younger was the illegitimate son of King Philip IV of Spain and an actress, recognised by his father and given high commands. In 1648 he recovered Naples from the revolutionary republic set up after Masaniello's revolt, and he later fought in Catalonia, the…

jayapura.s: Jayapura is the capital of the Indonesian province of Papua, on Yos Sudarso Bay on the north coast of New Guinea, near the border with Papua New Guinea. Founded by the Dutch in 1910 as Hollandia, it was the capital of Netherlands New Guinea and in 1944, after its capture from…

jean-talon.s: Jean Talon was the first intendant of New France, serving from 1665 to 1668 and from 1670 to 1672 under Louis XIV and his minister Colbert. He organised a census, encouraged the immigration of the filles du roi and large families, and promoted farming, shipbuilding, brewing…

john-davenport.s: John Davenport was an English Puritan minister who left London for New England in 1637 and in 1638 founded the New Haven Colony with the merchant Theophilus Eaton. He shaped its strict church-based government, in which only church members could vote.

jimmy-stevens.s: Jimmy Stevens was a ni-Vanuatu political leader who founded the Nagriamel movement on Espiritu Santo in the 1960s, campaigning for the return of land held by European planters. On the eve of independence in 1980 he led a secessionist rising on the island and declared the…

john-frum-movement.s: The John Frum movement is a religious movement on the island of Tanna in Vanuatu, often described as a cargo cult. It arose in the late 1930s around a figure called John Frum, who promised the islanders wealth if they abandoned missionary rule and returned to custom.

jose-sarney.s: José Sarney is a Brazilian politician and writer who was president of Brazil from 1985 to 1990, the first civilian president after the military dictatorship. Elected vice-president, he took office when Tancredo Neves fell ill and died.

johan-bjornsson-printz.s: Johan Björnsson Printz was a Swedish soldier who served as governor of New Sweden from 1643 to 1653. A veteran of the Thirty Years' War, he built Fort New Gothenburg on Tinicum Island as his seat, with other forts along the Delaware River, and traded with the Lenape and…

johan-risingh.s: Johan Risingh was a Swedish official and the last governor of New Sweden, from 1654 to 1655. On arriving he seized the Dutch Fort Casimir on the Delaware River and renamed it Fort Trinity.

jimyoin-line.s: The Jimyōin line was a branch of the Japanese imperial family descended from Emperor Go-Fukakusa, rival to the Daikakuji line of his brother Emperor Kameyama. From the late 13th century the two lines contested the throne, and the Kamakura shogunate arranged for them to alternate.

juqu-wuhui.s: Juqu Wuhui was a prince of the Northern Liang dynasty in north-western China, a son of Juqu Mengxun. After Northern Wei conquered the Northern Liang in 439, he and his brother Juqu Anzhou led the remnants of the family west, took Shanshan and in 442 Gaochang (Turpan), where…

junin-region.s: Junín is a region of central Peru, stretching from the Andean highlands around Lake Junín to the Amazonian forests of the east; its capital is Huancayo. Its high plateau was the scene of the Battle of Junín in August 1824, a cavalry victory of Simón Bolívar's forces over the…

jugurthine-war.s: The Jugurthine War was fought from 112 to 105 BCE between the Roman Republic and Jugurtha, king of Numidia. It began after Jugurtha seized Cirta and killed Adherbal and the Italian traders there, and Roman efforts were long hampered by bribery and defeats.

john-chilembwe.s: John Chilembwe was a Baptist minister and educator in Nyasaland, now Malawi. Educated in the United States, he founded the Providence Industrial Mission near Chiradzulu, and in January 1915 he led a short-lived rising against the abuses of British planters and colonial rule.

jurua-river.s: The Juruá River is a major southern tributary of the Amazon, rising in eastern Peru and flowing more than 3,000 km north-east through the Brazilian states of Acre and Amazonas to join the Solimões. Its basin was home to many indigenous peoples and was settled by rubber tappers…

johannes-brand.s: Johannes Brand was a Cape-born lawyer and politician who served as president of the Orange Free State from 1864 until his death in 1888. He led the republic through its wars with the Basotho in the 1860s and kept it neutral in the First Boer War.

jahangir-mahal.s: The Jahangir Mahal is a palace in Orchha, Madhya Pradesh, built in the early 17th century by Bir Singh Deo of Orchha. It is said to have been raised in honour of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, his patron and ally.

jaen.s: Jaén is a city in Andalusia, southern Spain, and the capital of the province of Jaén, below the castle hill of Santa Catalina. Under Muslim rule it was a fortress town and for a time the seat of a taifa, and in 1246 it was surrendered to Ferdinand III of Castile, becoming a…

jose-batlle-y-ordonez.s: José Batlle y Ordóñez was a Uruguayan journalist and Colorado Party politician, president in 1903–1907 and 1911–1915. He ended the last Blanco revolt in 1904 and built an early welfare state, introducing the eight-hour working day, secular education, divorce reform and…

jesus.s: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish preacher from Galilee whose life and teaching are the basis of Christianity. He taught in Galilee and the surrounding regions under Herod Antipas and was crucified at Jerusalem on the orders of the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, around 30–33 CE.

j-b-van-heutsz.s: J. B. van Heutsz was a Dutch general who brought the Aceh War to its decisive phase.

jan-van-swieten.s: Jan van Swieten was a Dutch general who commanded the second expedition against the Aceh Sultanate in 1873–1874, after the first had failed and its commander Köhler had been killed. His force captured the sultan's palace in January 1874, and he declared Aceh part of the Dutch…

johan-harmen-rudolf-kohler.s: Johan Harmen Rudolf Köhler was a Dutch major-general who led the first expedition against the Aceh Sultanate in April 1873, opening the Aceh War. His force landed near the capital but met fierce resistance, and Köhler was shot dead near the Great Mosque, the Masjid Raya…

jayadhwaj-singha.s: Jayadhwaj Singha was king of the Ahom kingdom of Assam from 1648 to 1663 and the first Ahom king to take initiation from a Vaishnavite satra. In 1662 the Mughal governor of Bengal, Mir Jumla, invaded, occupied the capital Garhgaon and forced him into the hills, and in 1663 he…

jorhat.s: Jorhat is a city in Upper Assam, north-east India, near the south bank of the Brahmaputra and the headquarters of Jorhat district. Gaurinath Singha moved the Ahom capital there in 1794, and it remained the seat of the last Ahom kings until the Burmese invasions.

jassic-people.s: The Jassic people, or Jász, were a group of Alan origin who settled in the Kingdom of Hungary in the thirteenth century, alongside the Cumans, after fleeing the Mongol invasions. They spoke an Iranian language related to Ossetian, recorded in a short fifteenth-century word…

jorge-luis-borges.s: Jorge Luis Borges was an Argentine writer whose short-story collections Ficciones (1944) and The Aleph (1949), with their labyrinths, mirrors and imaginary books, made him one of the most influential authors of the twentieth century. He was also a poet and essayist, and served…

jorge-rafael-videla.s: Jorge Rafael Videla was an Argentine general who led the military coup of 24 March 1976 and served as de facto president until 1981. His regime carried out the abduction, torture and killing of thousands of people in the Dirty War.

jose-felix-uriburu.s: José Félix Uriburu was an Argentine general who overthrew President Hipólito Yrigoyen on 6 September 1930 and ruled as de facto president until February 1932. He hoped to replace the democratic system with a corporatist order, but lost the support of the conservatives, who…

juan-bautista-alberdi.s: Juan Bautista Alberdi was an Argentine political theorist and diplomat of the Generation of 1837. His Bases and Starting Points for the Political Organisation of the Argentine Republic (1852) shaped the federal constitution adopted in 1853, and his maxim that 'to govern is to…

julio-cortazar.s: Julio Cortázar was an Argentine writer who lived in Paris from 1951 and became a leading figure of the Latin American Boom. He is best known for his experimental novel Hopscotch (1963), which can be read in more than one order, and for short stories such as 'Blow-Up', which…

jeongnimsa.s: Jeongnimsa is the site of a Buddhist temple in Buyeo, South Korea, built in the centre of Sabi, the last capital of Baekje, after the move there in 538. Its five-storey stone pagoda, one of only two surviving from Baekje, still stands.

james-heane.s: James Heane was an English Parliamentarian officer who, with Admiral Robert Blake, led the expedition that took Jersey from the royalists under Sir George Carteret in 1651. He then served as governor of the island.

jerriais.s: Jèrriais is the Norman language of Jersey, a variety of Norman French spoken on the island since the Middle Ages. It was the everyday language of most islanders until the twentieth century, while standard French served for law and government.

jersey-royal.s: The Jersey Royal is a variety of early new potato grown in Jersey, developed around 1880 by the farmer Hugh de la Haye from an unusually large potato with many eyes. Grown on the island's sloping south-facing côtils, it is exported to Britain each spring and became the chief…

jang-mun-hyu.s: Jang Mun-hyu was a general of Balhae who in 732, on the orders of King Mu, led a fleet across the Bohai Sea and attacked Dengzhou on the Shandong peninsula, killing its Tang prefect. The raid, part of a conflict caused by Balhae's war on the Heishui Mohe and the flight of…

jalaluddin-muhammad-shah.s: Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah, born Jadu, was sultan of Bengal and the son of the Hindu landholder Raja Ganesha. He converted to Islam and ruled from about 1415 to 1433, apart from a short period when his father returned to power.

jalaluddin-fath-shah.s: Jalaluddin Fath Shah was sultan of Bengal from 1481 to 1487, a member of the restored Ilyas Shahi dynasty. He tried to curb the power of the Abyssinian palace guards, who had grown strong under his predecessors, and was murdered by them in 1487.

james-robert-phillips.s: James Robert Phillips was a British colonial official, acting consul-general of the Niger Coast Protectorate. In January 1897 he led a small, largely unarmed party towards Benin City, intending to see the Oba, despite warnings to wait until a sacred festival had ended.

jama-masjid-bijapur.s: The Jama Masjid of Bijapur is the congregational mosque of the Adil Shahi capital, in present-day Karnataka, begun under Ali Adil Shah I in the later sixteenth century. Its large prayer hall under a broad central dome made it one of the biggest mosques in the Deccan.

jose-de-alencar.s: José de Alencar was a Brazilian novelist, playwright and politician, a leading figure of Brazilian Romanticism. His novels O Guarani (1857) and Iracema (1865) idealised the Indigenous peoples and the founding of Brazil, helping to create a national literature distinct from…

john-morley-1st-viscount-morley-of-black.n: John Morley, 1st Viscount Morley of Blackburn
john-morley-1st-viscount-morley-of-black.s: John Morley, 1st Viscount Morley of Blackburn, was a British Liberal politician, journalist and writer. A close ally and biographer of William Gladstone, he served as Chief Secretary for Ireland and, from 1905 to 1910, as Secretary of State for India, when with the Viceroy…

jallianwala-bagh-massacre.s: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, Punjab, when British Indian troops under Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired without warning on a large unarmed crowd in an enclosed garden. Official figures gave 379 dead, though Indian estimates were…

john-peters-humphrey.s: John Peters Humphrey was a Canadian legal scholar at McGill University who served as the first director of the Human Rights Division of the United Nations Secretariat from 1946 to 1966. He prepared the first draft of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948,…

juno-beach.s: Juno Beach was the code name of one of the five Allied landing sectors in Normandy on D-Day, 6 June 1944, stretching around Courseulles-sur-Mer. It was assaulted by the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division with British support, which overcame strong defences at a cost of more than a…

johann-caspar-lavater.s: Johann Caspar Lavater was a Swiss pastor, poet and writer from Zürich. His Essays on Physiognomy of 1775–1778, which claimed to read character from facial features, were famous across Europe and drew contributions from the young Goethe.

johann-heinrich-pestalozzi.s: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi was a Swiss educational reformer born in Zürich. In his novel Leonard and Gertrude and his schools for poor children, most famously at Yverdon from 1805, he argued that teaching should develop the whole child, 'head, heart and hand', through…

johann-jakob-bodmer.s: Johann Jakob Bodmer was a Swiss critic, scholar and teacher in Zürich. With Johann Jakob Breitinger he defended the role of imagination and the marvellous in poetry against the rationalist critic Gottsched.

johann-jakob-breitinger.s: Johann Jakob Breitinger was a Swiss philologist and critic who taught Hebrew and Greek in Zürich. His Critische Dichtkunst of 1740, written in alliance with Johann Jakob Bodmer, argued for imagination and feeling in poetry against the strict rules of Johann Christoph…

james-henry-craig.s: Sir James Henry Craig was a British general who commanded the troops that, with Admiral Elphinstone's fleet, took the Cape from the Dutch East India Company in 1795, and he governed the colony until 1797. He later served in India and the Mediterranean and was governor general…

jan-hendrik-hofmeyr-onze-jan.s: Jan Hendrik Hofmeyr, known as Onze Jan, was a Cape politician and journalist who led the Afrikaner Bond and was the most influential Afrikaner politician in the Cape Colony. He supported Cecil Rhodes's ministry until the Jameson Raid of 1895–1896 and campaigned for the…

john-molteno.s: Sir John Charles Molteno was a London-born Cape merchant and farmer who led the campaign for responsible government and became the first prime minister of the Cape Colony in 1872. His government built railways and resisted the British plan for a confederation of South Africa,…

john-philip-missionary.s: John Philip was a Scottish missionary who led the London Missionary Society in South Africa from 1819. He campaigned for the legal rights of the Khoikhoi, and his Researches in South Africa of 1828, with lobbying in London, helped secure Ordinance 50 and its confirmation by…

john-tengo-jabavu.s: John Tengo Jabavu was a Xhosa journalist and political leader in the Cape Colony, educated at the Healdtown mission. In 1884 he founded Imvo Zabantsundu, the first newspaper owned and edited by a black South African, and he used the Cape's qualified franchise to organise…

john-x-merriman.s: John X. Merriman was an English-born Cape politician who served in many ministries and was the last prime minister of the Cape Colony, from 1908 to 1910.

james-stanislaus-bell.s: James Stanislaus Bell was a British merchant who in 1836 sent the schooner Vixen to the Circassian coast to challenge Russia's blockade, provoking the Vixen affair. He then lived among the Circassians from 1837 to 1839, supporting their resistance, and published a Journal of a…

jack-lang.s: Jack Lang was a Labor premier of New South Wales from 1925 to 1927 and from 1930 to 1932. During the Great Depression his Lang Plan called for suspending interest payments to British bondholders, and his government defaulted on payments to the Commonwealth.

james-scullin.s: James Scullin was the Labor prime minister of Australia from 1929 to 1932, taking office just before the Wall Street Crash. His government struggled with the Great Depression, falling export prices and heavy debts, and the Labor Party split over the response.

john-monash.s: Sir John Monash was an Australian civil engineer and general. After commanding a brigade at Gallipoli and a division in France, he led the Australian Corps from May 1918, planning the battle of Hamel and leading his corps in the Allied offensives of the last months of the war,…

john-boyd-dunlop.s: John Boyd Dunlop was a Scottish-born veterinary surgeon in Belfast who in 1888 developed a practical pneumatic tyre, first for his son's tricycle. Its rapid adoption for bicycles and then motor cars created a huge world demand for rubber, which drove the brutal exploitation of…

joseph-conrad.s: Joseph Conrad was a Polish-born British novelist, born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski, who served for years as a merchant seaman before turning to writing in English. His works, including Lord Jim, Nostromo and Heart of Darkness, explore moral ambiguity and empire.

jacob-van-artevelde.s: Jacob van Artevelde was a wealthy citizen of Ghent who from 1338 led the city and, in effect, much of the County of Flanders. To keep English wool flowing to the Flemish cloth industry, he took Flanders into alliance with Edward III at the start of the Hundred Years' War, and…

jean-froissart.s: Jean Froissart was a poet and chronicler from Valenciennes in Hainaut. He entered the service of Philippa of Hainaut, queen of England, in the 1360s and later found patrons in the Low Countries and France.

jemmapes-department.s: Jemmapes was a department of the French Republic and Empire, created in 1795 from the County of Hainaut and neighbouring lands after the annexation of the Austrian Netherlands. Named after the French victory at Jemappes in 1792, it had its capital at Mons.

john-ii-count-of-holland.s: John II of Avesnes was count of Hainaut from 1280 and of Holland and Zeeland from 1299 until his death in 1304. A grandson of Countess Margaret II of Flanders and Hainaut by her first marriage, he inherited Holland and Zeeland from his young cousin John I.

john-of-gaunt.s: John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, was the third surviving son of Edward III of England and Philippa of Hainaut, born at Ghent. The richest magnate in England, he dominated government during the minority of his nephew Richard II and claimed the crown of Castile through his…

joan-of-england-queen-of-sicily.n: Joan of England, Queen of Sicily
joan-of-england-queen-of-sicily.s: Joan of England was a daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. She married King William II of Sicily in 1177 and, after his death, was freed by her brother Richard I, whom she accompanied on the Third Crusade.

juan-de-lanuza-y-urrea.s: Juan de Lanuza y Urrea was the Justicia of Aragon, the judge charged with upholding the kingdom's fueros against royal power. When Philip II tried to seize his fugitive secretary Antonio Pérez in Zaragoza in 1591, Lanuza called the Aragonese to resist; a royal army entered the…

justicia-of-aragon.s: The Justicia of Aragon was a high judge of the medieval Kingdom of Aragon who arbitrated between the king and his subjects and could protect individuals against royal officials. From the late 13th century the office became the guardian of Aragonese liberties.

john-i-of-castile.s: John I was king of Castile from 1379 to 1390, the son of Henry II and second king of the House of Trastámara. Married to Beatrice of Portugal, he claimed the Portuguese throne in 1383, but his army was defeated at Aljubarrota in 1385 by John I of Portugal.

joanna-la-beltraneja.s: Joanna la Beltraneja was the daughter of Henry IV of Castile, whose enemies claimed she was the child of the courtier Beltrán de la Cueva. Backed by her uncle Afonso V of Portugal, she contested the throne with Isabella I in the War of the Castilian Succession of 1475–1479.

jan-palach.s: Jan Palach was a Czech student who set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square in Prague on 16 January 1969 in protest against the public's resignation after the Warsaw Pact invasion. He died three days later, and his funeral became a mass demonstration.

jaroslav-hasek.s: Jaroslav Hašek was a Czech writer and humorist, best known for his unfinished comic novel The Good Soldier Švejk, published from 1921 to 1923. Drawing on his own service in the Austro-Hungarian army and as a prisoner in Russia, it satirises military bureaucracy and war, and it…

johann-friedrich-struensee.s: Johann Friedrich Struensee was a German physician who became royal doctor to the mentally ill Christian VII of Denmark and the lover of Queen Caroline Matilda. From 1770 to 1772 he ruled Denmark-Norway in the king's name, issuing hundreds of Enlightenment decrees, including…

john-talbot-1st-earl-of-shrewsbury.s: John Talbot, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, was an English soldier and the most famous English commander of the later Hundred Years' War. Captured at Patay in 1429 and created Earl of Shrewsbury in 1442, he fought for decades in Normandy and northern France.

jan-van-ruusbroec.s: Jan van Ruusbroec was a Brabantine mystic and priest of Brussels who withdrew in 1343 to Groenendaal in the Sonian Forest, where he became prior of a community of canons regular and died in 1381. His Middle Dutch works, above all The Spiritual Espousals, describe the stages of…

jean-bourdichon.s: Jean Bourdichon was a French painter and illuminator from Tours who served four kings of France, Louis XI, Charles VIII, Louis XII and Francis I. His best-known work is the Grandes Heures of Anne of Brittany, painted about 1503–1508, with its lifelike plants and insects in the…

joan-of-penthievre.s: Joan of Penthièvre was a Breton noblewoman, niece of Duke John III and countess of Penthièvre, whose claim to Brittany was pressed by her husband Charles of Blois in the War of the Breton Succession. After Charles was killed at Auray in 1364, the First Treaty of Guérande left…

john-v-duke-of-brittany.s: John V was duke of Brittany from 1399 to 1442, the son of John IV. He kept Brittany largely out of the later Hundred Years' War, shifting between England and France, and survived his kidnapping by the rival Penthièvre family in 1420.

joan-iii-countess-of-burgundy.s: Joan III was countess of Burgundy (the Franche-Comté) and of Artois from 1330 until her death in 1347, the eldest daughter of King Philip V of France. In 1318 she married Duke Odo IV of Burgundy, uniting the duchy and the Free County of Burgundy under one ruling couple.

john-the-fearless.s: John the Fearless was duke of Burgundy from 1404 until 1419, the son of Philip the Bold. Captured at Nicopolis in 1396 and victor over Liège at Othée in 1408, he had Louis of Orléans murdered in 1407, which began the civil war between Burgundians and Armagnacs.

jacques-callot.s: Jacques Callot was a printmaker and draughtsman from Nancy in the Duchy of Lorraine who worked in Florence for the Medici before returning home around 1621. He produced more than 1,400 etchings and greatly refined the technique.

jean-lamour.s: Jean Lamour was a locksmith and ironworker from Nancy who worked for Stanisław Leszczyński, duke of Lorraine and Bar. He made the gilded wrought-iron gates, railings and lanterns of the Place Royale, now Place Stanislas, in Nancy, completed in 1755.

joan-of-arc.s: Joan of Arc was a peasant girl from Domrémy, on the borders of Lorraine and Champagne, who believed that saints' voices called her to save France in the Hundred Years' War. In 1429 she helped lift the English siege of Orléans and brought Charles VII to his coronation at Reims.

johan-de-witt.s: Johan de Witt was Grand Pensionary of Holland from 1653 to 1672 and the leading statesman of the Dutch Republic during the First Stadtholderless Period. A skilled mathematician and financier, he restored the Republic's finances, built up its navy and kept the house of Orange…

johan-van-oldenbarnevelt.s: Johan van Oldenbarnevelt was Land's Advocate of Holland from 1586 and the leading statesman of the young Dutch Republic. He organised its finances and government, helped found the Dutch East India Company in 1602 and negotiated the Twelve Years' Truce with Spain in 1609.

judicial-papyrus-of-turin.s: The Judicial Papyrus of Turin is an Egyptian papyrus of the twelfth century BCE recording the trials of those accused in the harem conspiracy against Ramesses III. It lists dozens of defendants, including a royal son, women of the harem, officials and guards, with the…

john-casimir-of-the-palatinate-simmern.s: John Casimir was a Calvinist prince of the Palatinate, a younger son of Elector Frederick III. He led German mercenary armies to aid the Huguenots in the French Wars of Religion, notably in 1567–1568 and 1575–1576, and intervened in the Dutch Revolt.

johann-friedrich-bottger.s: Johann Friedrich Böttger was a German alchemist held at the court of Augustus the Strong, who expected him to make gold. Working with Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus in Dresden, he produced Europe's first true hard-paste porcelain around 1708–1709 and became the first…

john-george-iii-elector-of-saxony.n: John George III, Elector of Saxony
john-george-iii-elector-of-saxony.s: John George III was Elector of Saxony from 1680 to 1691. He created Saxony's first standing army and led Saxon troops at the relief of Vienna in 1683, fighting alongside John III Sobieski against the Ottomans, and later commanded imperial forces on the Rhine against France in…

john-ii-of-castile.s: John II was King of Castile from 1406 to 1454, succeeding his father Henry III as an infant under the regency of his mother and his uncle Ferdinand. His long reign was dominated by his favourite Álvaro de Luna, whom he finally had executed in 1453, and by conflict with the…

jandarids.s: The Jandarids, also called Isfendiyarids, were a Turkmen dynasty that ruled a beylik in northern Anatolia centred on Kastamonu and the Black Sea port of Sinop from about 1292 to 1461. They long survived between the Ottomans and other Anatolian powers, but the last ruler,…

jose-cecilio-del-valle.s: José Cecilio del Valle (1780–1834) was a Honduran lawyer, journalist and politician who is credited with drafting the Central American declaration of independence of 15 September 1821. A leading figure in the politics of the federation, he won the presidential election of 1834…

juan-barrundia.s: Juan Barrundia was a Guatemalan liberal politician and the first head of the State of Guatemala within the Federal Republic of Central America, from 1824. His arrest in September 1826 on the orders of the federal president Manuel José Arce broke the liberal alliance and set…

john-the-exarch.s: John the Exarch was a Bulgarian scholar and churchman of the late 9th and early 10th centuries, active at Preslav under Simeon I. His Hexaemeron, a commentary on the six days of creation drawn from Greek sources, includes a celebrated description of Simeon's court.

johan-van-valckenburgh.s: Johan van Valckenburgh (c. 1575–1625) was a Dutch military engineer who designed fortifications for several northern European cities.

jacques-massu.s: Jacques Massu (1908–2002) was a French general who had served with the Free French in the Second World War. Commanding the 10th Parachute Division, he was given police powers in Algiers in 1957 and broke the FLN network in the Battle of Algiers through mass arrests and torture.

jonnart-law.s: The Jonnart Law of February 1919, named after the governor-general Charles Jonnart, widened the rights of Muslim Algerians after their service in the First World War. It eased access to French citizenship and enlarged the Muslim electorate for local assemblies, while keeping…

jacques-louis-randon.s: Jacques Louis Randon (1795–1871) was a French general and marshal who served as governor-general of Algeria from 1851 to 1858. His campaign of 1857 subdued Great Kabylia, completing the conquest of the mountains of northern Algeria, and he founded Fort-Napoléon there.

jean-decoux.s: Jean Decoux was a French admiral who governed French Indochina for the Vichy regime from 1940 to 1945. He accepted the stationing of Japanese troops in the colony while keeping French administration in place, and promoted youth, sports and local patriotic movements loyal to…

joost-van-vollenhoven.s: Joost van Vollenhoven was a Dutch-born French colonial administrator who became governor-general of French West Africa in 1917. He resigned the same year in protest against renewed mass recruitment of African soldiers for the First World War, which he believed would ruin the…

james-bruce.s: James Bruce was a Scottish explorer who spent several years in Ethiopia and in 1770 reached the source of the Blue Nile near Lake Tana. On his return journey in 1772 he passed through Sennar and left one of the few eyewitness accounts of the Funj court.

julius-maternus.s: Julius Maternus was a Roman traveller who, according to Ptolemy's Geography citing Marinus of Tyre, journeyed with the king of the Garamantes on an expedition south from the Fezzan to the land of Agisymba, said to have taken four months, in the late first century CE. His…

jeong-jung-bu.s: Jeong Jung-bu was a Korean general who led the military coup of 1170 in Goryeo. Angered by the contempt of civil officials, his officers massacred courtiers, deposed King Uijong and set up King Myeongjong, beginning a century of military rule.

jeong-mong-ju.s: Jeong Mong-ju was a Korean Neo-Confucian scholar, diplomat and statesman of the late Goryeo period. He led missions to Ming China and Japan and promoted Confucian ritual and education.

jinul.s: Jinul was a Korean Buddhist monk of the Goryeo period who reformed Seon (Zen) Buddhism. He founded a community at Songgwangsa and taught that sudden awakening should be followed by gradual cultivation, joining meditation with doctrinal study.

jose-maria-cordova.s: José María Córdova was a general of the wars of independence from Antioquia in New Granada. He distinguished himself at Boyacá and especially at Ayacucho in 1824, where he led the decisive attack.

jose-prudencio-padilla.s: José Prudencio Padilla was an admiral of Gran Colombia, born in Riohacha of African and indigenous descent. He had served in the Spanish navy before joining the patriots, and in 1823 he won the naval Battle of Lake Maracaibo, ending Spanish power in Venezuela.

justus-von-liebig.s: Justus von Liebig was a German chemist, born in Darmstadt, who was professor at the University of Giessen from 1824 to 1852 and then at Munich. His teaching laboratory at Giessen trained students from across Europe and America and became a model for chemical education.

joseph-maria-olbrich.s: Joseph Maria Olbrich was an Austrian architect and a founder of the Vienna Secession, whose exhibition building in Vienna he designed in 1897-1898. Invited by Grand Duke Ernest Louis to the Darmstadt Artists' Colony in 1899, he designed most of its buildings on the…

janusz-radziwill.s: Janusz Radziwiłł was a Lithuanian magnate, Calvinist leader and Grand Hetman of Lithuania. During the Russian and Swedish invasions of 1655 he signed the Union of Kėdainiai, placing the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under the protection of Charles X Gustav of Sweden.

jacques-santer.s: Jacques Santer is a Luxembourg Christian Social politician who was prime minister from 1984 to 1995 and President of the European Commission from 1995 to 1999. His Commission prepared the introduction of the euro, but in March 1999 it resigned collectively after an independent…

jean-claude-juncker.s: Jean-Claude Juncker is a Luxembourg Christian Social politician who was prime minister from 1995 to 2013, by then the longest-serving head of government in the European Union. He chaired the Eurogroup of eurozone finance ministers from 2005 to 2013 and served as President of…

joseph-bech.s: Joseph Bech was a Luxembourg Christian Social statesman who was prime minister from 1926 to 1937 and again from 1953 to 1958, and foreign minister for most of the years from 1926 to 1959. He led Luxembourg's diplomacy in exile during the Second World War, helped create the…

jonah-metropolitan-of-moscow.s: Jonah was a Russian churchman elected Metropolitan of Kiev and All Rus' by a council of Russian bishops in Moscow in 1448, without the approval of the Patriarch of Constantinople. His election, made after Moscow rejected the union with Rome agreed at the Council of Florence,…

jacopo-peri.s: Jacopo Peri was a Florentine composer and singer associated with the Florentine Camerata and the Medici court. His Dafne of about 1598, now largely lost, is regarded as the first opera, and his Euridice, performed at the Pitti Palace in 1600 for the wedding of Maria de' Medici…

jachymov.s: Jáchymov, in German Joachimsthal, is a town in the Ore Mountains of north-western Czechia, founded after rich silver deposits were found there in 1516. The Counts Schlick minted large silver coins there from 1520, the Joachimsthaler, whose name, shortened to thaler, gave rise…

johann-bernhard-fischer-von-erlach.s: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach was an Austrian architect, the leading master of Habsburg Baroque. Trained in Rome, he worked for the imperial court in Vienna, designing the Karlskirche, the Court Library in the Hofburg and the first plans for Schönbrunn Palace, as well as…

johann-lukas-von-hildebrandt.s: Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt was an Austrian Baroque architect, born in Genoa, who became court architect in Vienna. His masterpiece is the Belvedere, built for Prince Eugene of Savoy between 1714 and 1723, and he also worked on the Schwarzenberg Palace in Vienna and the…

joseph-haydn.s: Joseph Haydn was an Austrian composer, one of the founders of the Classical style. For nearly thirty years he served the Esterházy princes, developing the symphony and the string quartet, and he later won great success in London.

josephinism.s: Josephinism is the name given to the policies of Joseph II of the Habsburg Monarchy and the tradition they created. It subordinated the Catholic Church to the state, dissolving hundreds of contemplative monasteries, granting toleration to Protestants, Orthodox Christians and…

john-of-the-cross.s: John of the Cross was a Spanish Carmelite friar, priest and mystic who worked with Teresa of Ávila to reform the Carmelite order. Imprisoned by opponents of the reform in Toledo in 1577–1578, he composed there part of his Spiritual Canticle.

juan-gines-de-sepulveda.s: Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda was a Spanish humanist, philosopher and royal chronicler. Drawing on Aristotle's idea of natural slavery, he argued that the Spanish conquest of the Americas was just, because the indigenous peoples were barbarous and could be subjected for their own good.

john-of-austria.s: John of Austria was an illegitimate son of the Emperor Charles V, recognised by his half-brother Philip II of Spain. He suppressed the Morisco revolt of the Alpujarras in 1568–1571 and commanded the fleet of the Holy League that defeated the Ottomans at Lepanto in 1571.

jakob-fugger.s: Jakob Fugger was a merchant and banker of Augsburg who made the Fugger firm the leading financial house of Europe. Through loans to the Habsburgs he gained control of silver and copper mines in Tyrol and Hungary, and he financed the election of Charles V as emperor in 1519.

janna.s: Janna was a Kannada poet at the court of the Hoysala kings Veera Ballala II and Narasimha II. His best-known works are the Yashodhara Charite of 1209, a Jain moral tale, and the Anantanatha Purana of 1230.

john-howland-rowe.s: John Howland Rowe was an American archaeologist and anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was one of the founders of modern Andean studies. Working from Spanish chronicles, notably Miguel Cabello de Balboa, he set out the widely used chronology of Inca…

juan-de-betanzos.s: Juan de Betanzos was a Spanish chronicler and interpreter of Quechua in early colonial Peru. Married to Cuxirimay Ocllo, a noblewoman of Atahualpa's family, he drew on the memories of her relatives for his Suma y narración de los Incas, completed in 1551, one of the earliest…

joko-widodo.s: Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi, is an Indonesian politician who served as president from 2014 to 2024. A furniture exporter from Surakarta, he became mayor of that city and governor of Jakarta before winning the presidency as the first leader from outside the political and…

jacques-rene-de-brisay-de-denonville.s: Jacques-René de Brisay, Marquis de Denonville, was governor general of New France from 1685 to 1689. In 1687, after seizing Iroquois men at Fort Frontenac and sending some to the galleys in France, he invaded the country of the Seneca and burned their villages and crops.

jianzhou-jurchens.s: The Jianzhou Jurchens were one of the three main groups into which the Ming dynasty divided the Jurchen peoples of Manchuria, living in the mountains east of Liaodong. From 1583 their chief Nurhaci united the Jianzhou and then the other Jurchen groups, organising them into the…

johor-river.s: The Johor River flows about 120 kilometres south-east through the Malaysian state of Johor into the Johor Strait. After the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511, the exiled sultans built a succession of capitals along it, among them Johor Lama and Kota Tinggi, which made the river…

jang-yeong-sil.s: Jang Yeong-sil was a Korean engineer and inventor of the early Joseon dynasty. Born of low status, he was promoted to high office by King Sejong for his skill.

jeong-do-jeon.s: Jeong Do-jeon was a Korean Neo-Confucian scholar and statesman who was the chief architect of the Joseon dynasty. He helped Yi Seong-gye seize power from Goryeo, drafted the land reform of 1391, designed the new capital at Hanyang and wrote the first codes of Joseon government.

jeong-yak-yong.s: Jeong Yak-yong, known as Dasan, was a Korean scholar and official, the leading figure of the Practical Learning (silhak) school. Favoured by King Jeongjo, he helped design the construction of Hwaseong Fortress.

janke-waali.s: Janke Waali was the last mansaba, or paramount ruler, of the Mandinka Kaabu Empire in present-day Guinea-Bissau and Senegal. In 1867 the forces of the Fula state of Futa Jallon besieged his capital Kansala.

jahangir-khan.s: Jahangir Khan was khan of the Kazakhs from 1628 to 1652 and a son of Esim Khan. In 1643, with a small force armed with muskets and help from Yalangtush Bahadur of Samarkand, he is said to have checked the Dzungar ruler Erdeni Batur at the Battle of Orbulaq in the mountains of…

jugend-magazine.s: Jugend was an illustrated weekly magazine of art and literature founded in Munich in 1896 by the publisher Georg Hirth. Known for its decorative covers and satirical tone, it gave its name to Jugendstil, the German form of Art Nouveau.

james-ensor.s: James Ensor was a Belgian painter and printmaker from Ostend, a forerunner of expressionism. He was a member of the avant-garde group Les XX, and his works, filled with masks, skeletons and crowds, mocked bourgeois society.

john-cockerill.s: John Cockerill was an English-born industrialist who became a pioneer of the Industrial Revolution on the Continent. In 1817 he set up an ironworks and machine factory at Seraing near Liège, which grew into one of the largest industrial concerns in Europe, building steam…

jan-zizka.s: Jan Žižka was a Czech general and leader of the Hussites. Blind in one eye and later in both, he organised armies of townsmen and peasants that used war wagons formed into laagers, together with early firearms.

john-amos-comenius.s: John Amos Comenius was a Czech philosopher, educator and the last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren. Driven into exile after the Battle of White Mountain, he lived in Poland, Sweden, England and finally Amsterdam.

john-wycliffe.s: John Wycliffe was an English theologian and Oxford scholar who attacked the wealth and authority of the Church, questioned transubstantiation and held that Scripture was the supreme authority. He inspired the first complete translation of the Bible into English and the Lollard…

james-hannington.s: James Hannington was an English Anglican missionary and the first bishop of Eastern Equatorial Africa. In 1885 he tried to reach Buganda by the eastern route through Busoga, which the Baganda feared as the direction of invasion.

junju-of-buganda.s: Junju was kabaka of Buganda in the second half of the eighteenth century. In his reign Buganda conquered the rich province of Buddu from Bunyoro, extending the kingdom along the western shore of Lake Victoria and gaining access to the trade and ironworking of the south-west.

john-beattie.s: John Beattie was a British social anthropologist at the University of Oxford, known for his fieldwork among the Nyoro of western Uganda in the 1950s. His books "Bunyoro: An African Kingdom" (1960) and "The Nyoro State" (1971) became standard studies of an African kingdom, and…

jutland-code.s: The Jutland Code is a medieval law code issued by King Valdemar II of Denmark in 1241, valid for Jutland, Funen and Schleswig. It opens with the words "with law shall the land be built" and covered land, inheritance, crime and procedure.

jules-mazarin.s: Jules Mazarin was an Italian-born cardinal and diplomat who served as chief minister of France from 1642 until his death in 1661. Succeeding Richelieu, he governed for the young Louis XIV with the regent Anne of Austria, survived the revolts of the Fronde and secured French…

jean-racine.s: Jean Racine was a French dramatist, the leading writer of tragedy in the age of Louis XIV. Educated by the Jansenists of Port-Royal, he wrote plays such as Andromaque, Britannicus and Phèdre, which follow the classical rules of unity in elegant verse.

james-francis-edward-stuart.s: James Francis Edward Stuart, known as the Old Pretender, was the son of the Catholic James II of England and the Jacobite claimant to the thrones of England, Scotland and Ireland. His birth in 1688 helped provoke the Glorious Revolution, and he was raised in exile in France.

james-hargreaves.s: James Hargreaves was an English weaver and carpenter from Lancashire who invented the spinning jenny around 1764. The machine let one worker spin several threads at once and greatly increased the output of cotton yarn in domestic production.

james-watt.s: James Watt was a Scottish inventor and instrument maker whose improvements made the steam engine practical for industry. His separate condenser, patented in 1769, greatly reduced fuel consumption, and in partnership with Matthew Boulton at Birmingham from 1775 he built engines…

john-churchill-1st-duke-of-marlborough.s: John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, was an English general and statesman who commanded the allied armies against France in the War of the Spanish Succession. His victories at Blenheim in 1704, Ramillies in 1706, Oudenarde in 1708 and Malplaquet in 1709 made Britain a…

john-of-capistrano.s: John of Capistrano was an Italian Franciscan friar and preacher who campaigned across central Europe against the Hussites and for a crusade against the Ottomans. In 1456 he raised a crusading army of peasants and townsmen that, with John Hunyadi's forces, broke the Ottoman…

jean-chardin.s: Jean Chardin was a French jeweller and traveller who made two long journeys to Safavid Persia between 1665 and 1677, passing through Mingrelia, Imereti and Georgia in 1672–1673. His account, published from 1686, is one of the most detailed European descriptions of Safavid Iran…

jean-joseph-amable-humbert.s: Jean Joseph Amable Humbert was a French general of the Revolutionary Wars. In August 1798 he landed at Killala in County Mayo with about a thousand troops to support the Irish rebellion and routed government forces at Castlebar, but he surrendered to Lord Cornwallis at…

jeroboam-ii.s: Jeroboam II was king of Israel in the first half of the eighth century BCE, reigning about forty years according to the Books of Kings. Taking advantage of the weakness of Aram-Damascus after Assyrian attacks, he restored Israel's borders and presided over its greatest…

jezebel.s: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess, the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, who married King Ahab of Israel in the ninth century BCE. The Books of Kings portray her as a promoter of the worship of Baal and an enemy of the prophet Elijah, and tell how she was thrown from…

jezreel-city.s: Jezreel was an ancient city in the north of the Kingdom of Israel, on a ridge overlooking the Jezreel Valley. Excavations at Tel Jezreel have revealed a large fortified royal enclosure of the ninth century BCE, built by the Omride kings as a second residence and military base.

jezreel-valley.s: The Jezreel Valley is a broad fertile plain in northern Israel, between the hills of Galilee and Samaria, running from Mount Carmel towards the Jordan. The main route from Egypt to Syria crossed it past Megiddo, which made it one of the great battlefields of the ancient Near…

jehoash-of-israel.s: Jehoash, or Joash, was king of Israel in the early eighth century BCE, the grandson of Jehu. Taking advantage of Assyrian pressure on Damascus, he defeated the Arameans three times and recovered towns lost by his father, and he defeated and captured Amaziah of Judah at…

jehoram-of-israel.s: Jehoram, or Joram, was king of Israel in the mid-ninth century BCE, the son of Ahab and the last king of the House of Omri. He failed to reconquer Moab after the revolt of Mesha and fought the Arameans of Hazael at Ramoth-gilead.

jehoahaz-of-judah.s: Jehoahaz was king of Judah for three months in 609 BCE, a son of Josiah. After Josiah was killed at Megiddo the people of the land made Jehoahaz king, but the pharaoh Necho II deposed him and took him to Egypt, where he died.

jehoahaz-of-israel.s: Jehoahaz was king of Israel in the late 9th century BCE, the son of Jehu. According to the Bible his reign saw heavy defeats by Hazael and Ben-Hadad of Aram-Damascus, which left him with only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and 10,000 foot soldiers.

jehoiada.s: Jehoiada was a priest in Jerusalem in the 9th century BCE who, according to the Bible, led the coup that overthrew Queen Athaliah. He had hidden the young prince Joash in the temple for six years, then crowned him with the help of the royal guard and had Athaliah killed.

jehoiakim.s: Jehoiakim was king of Judah from 609 to 598 BCE, a son of Josiah. The pharaoh Necho II installed him in place of his brother Jehoahaz, and after Nebuchadnezzar II defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BCE he submitted to Babylon.

jehoram-of-judah.s: Jehoram was king of Judah in the mid-9th century BCE, the son of Jehoshaphat. His marriage to Athaliah, daughter of the house of Omri, sealed the alliance with Israel.

jehoshaphat.s: Jehoshaphat was king of Judah in the first half of the 9th century BCE, the son of Asa. He made peace with Israel, allied with Ahab and married his son Jehoram to Athaliah of the house of Omri, and he fought beside Israel's kings against Aram and Moab.

joash-of-judah.s: Joash, also called Jehoash, was king of Judah in the late 9th and early 8th centuries BCE. According to the Bible he was hidden as an infant when his grandmother Athaliah killed the royal family, and crowned at the age of seven by the priest Jehoiada.
