jarasandha.s: Jarasandha is a legendary king of Magadha in the Mahabharata and the Puranas, of the Brihadratha dynasty. In the epic he is a powerful enemy of Krishna who drives the Yadavas from Mathura, and he is killed in a wrestling match by the Pandava prince Bhima.

joanna-ii-of-naples.s: Joanna II (1373–1435) was queen of Naples from 1414 to 1435, succeeding her brother Ladislaus as the last ruler of the Angevin Durazzo line. Her reign was dominated by favourites and shifting alliances, and she adopted in turn Alfonso V of Aragon and Louis III of Anjou as heirs.

januarius.s: Januarius (San Gennaro) was a bishop of Benevento martyred around 305, probably in the persecution of Diocletian. He is the patron saint of Naples, where a vial of what is believed to be his dried blood is kept in the cathedral.

jean-andoche-junot.s: Jean-Andoche Junot was a French general and early comrade of Napoleon Bonaparte. In November 1807 he led the invasion of Portugal, reaching Lisbon just after the royal court had sailed for Brazil, and was made Duke of Abrantes.

joao-das-regras.s: João das Regras was a Portuguese jurist trained in Roman law at Bologna. At the Cortes of Coimbra in 1385 he argued that the throne was vacant and that the rival claimants had no valid right, persuading the assembly to elect John, Master of Aviz, as King John I.

james-ii-of-scotland.s: James II was King of Scots from 1437 to 1460, known for the red birthmark on his face. After a minority dominated by noble factions, he broke the power of the Black Douglases, killing the eighth earl in 1452.

john-barbour.s: John Barbour was a Scottish poet and churchman, archdeacon of Aberdeen from 1357. His verse epic The Brus, completed around 1375, tells the story of Robert the Bruce and the Wars of Independence and is the first major work of literature in Scots.

john-knox.s: John Knox was the leading figure of the Scottish Reformation. After serving as a galley slave in France and as a minister in England, he worked with Calvin in Geneva, and on his return in 1559 his preaching helped spark the Protestant revolt.

juliana-of-the-netherlands.s: Juliana was Queen of the Netherlands from 1948 to 1980, succeeding her mother Wilhelmina. During the Second World War she lived in exile in Canada.

jarrow.s: Jarrow is a town on the south bank of the River Tyne in north-east England. Its monastery of St Paul, founded by Benedict Biscop in the early 680s and joined with Wearmouth, was a centre of Northumbrian learning where Bede lived and wrote, and the dedication stone of its…

justinus-kerner.s: Justinus Kerner was a German poet and physician from Ludwigsburg, a leading member of the Swabian school of poets alongside Ludwig Uhland. As a doctor at Weinsberg he gave the first detailed description of botulism, caused by spoiled sausages, and he wrote widely on the…

jaga.s: The Jaga were invaders who overran the Kingdom of Kongo in 1568, sacking São Salvador and forcing King Álvaro I to flee, until a Portuguese expedition helped to expel them in the early 1570s. Their origin is debated: historians have identified them with peoples from the east…

jebel-barkal.s: Jebel Barkal is a flat-topped sandstone mountain near Karima in northern Sudan, held sacred as a home of the god Amun. Egyptian kings of the New Kingdom built a temple at its foot, and the Kushite kings of Napata enlarged it as the religious centre of their state; Piye set up…

jinakalamali.s: The Jinakalamali is a Pali chronicle written by the monk Ratanapanna at Chiang Mai, completed in 1516–1517 under King Phra Mueang Kaeo. It traces the history of Buddhism from the Buddha to Lan Na, including the coming of the Sri Lankan monastic lineages and the deeds of the…

jiaozhi.s: Jiaozhi was the Chinese name for the region of the Red River delta in northern Vietnam. It was a commandery under the Han dynasty after 111 BCE and, much later, a province of the Ming Empire from 1407, when the Yongle Emperor annexed Đại Việt, until 1427, when Lê Lợi's…

jatavarman-kulasekara-i.s: Jatavarman Kulasekara I was a Pandya king of Madurai who reigned from 1190 to 1216, as the Pandyas began to emerge from long subordination to the Cholas. His attempt to assert independence was crushed by the Chola king Kulottunga III, who invaded the Pandya country and sacked…

jaffna-kingdom.s: The Jaffna Kingdom was a Tamil kingdom in northern Sri Lanka ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty, whose origins are connected with the Pandya expeditions to the island in the late 13th century. Centred on the Jaffna peninsula, it controlled the pearl fisheries at times and…

jamal-al-din-astronomer.s: Jamal al-Din was a Persian astronomer who served the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan. In 1267 he presented a calendar and a set of astronomical instruments, including an armillary sphere and a celestial globe, to the court, and he later headed the Islamic astronomical observatory in…

joseph-boakai.s: Joseph Boakai is a Liberian politician who was vice-president under Ellen Johnson Sirleaf from 2006 to 2018. After losing the 2017 election to George Weah, he defeated him in 2023 and became president in January 2024, in a peaceful transfer of power.

john-of-biclaro.s: John of Biclaro was a Hispano-Roman chronicler and bishop of Girona, born at Scallabis (Santarém) in Lusitania. He spent some seventeen years in Constantinople and, after exile under the Arian Visigothic king Leovigild, founded the monastery of Biclaro.

justin-ii.s: Justin II was Byzantine emperor from 565 to 578, nephew and successor of Justinian I. He refused payments to the Avars and Persia, and his reign saw the Lombard invasion of Italy in 568 and a renewed war with Persia in which the fortress of Dara fell in 573.

jacob-zuma.s: Jacob Zuma is a South African politician who was president of South Africa from 2009 to 2018 and leader of the African National Congress from 2007 to 2017. A former anti-apartheid activist imprisoned on Robben Island, he presided over a government marked by corruption and…

john-cicero.s: John Cicero was Elector of Brandenburg from 1486 to 1499, son of Albert Achilles. He was the first elector to reside permanently in Berlin, making it the capital of the Mark, and he introduced an excise on beer.

john-sigismund-elector-of-brandenburg.s: John Sigismund was Elector of Brandenburg from 1608 to 1619. Through his marriage to Anna of Prussia he acquired claims to the Jülich–Cleves inheritance, gaining Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg by the Treaty of Xanten in 1614, and in 1618 he inherited the Duchy of Prussia.

jihlava.s: Jihlava is a city in the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands of the Czech Republic, on the historic border between Bohemia and Moravia. It grew into a royal town in the 13th century after silver was found there, becoming one of the richest towns of the Czech lands, and its mining law…

john-henry-margrave-of-moravia.s: John Henry, Margrave of Moravia, was a younger son of King John of Bohemia and brother of Emperor Charles IV. Briefly the husband of Margaret Maultasch and nominal count of Tyrol until she expelled him in 1341, he received Moravia from Charles as a fief in 1349 and ruled it…

jean-claude-margueron.s: Jean-Claude Margueron is a French archaeologist who directed the excavations at Mari in Syria from 1979 to 2004, succeeding André Parrot. His work reconstructed the origins of the city as a planned circular settlement of the early third millennium BCE, with flood defences and…

javanese-calendar.s: The Javanese calendar was introduced by Sultan Agung of Mataram in 1633. It kept the year count of the old Saka era but replaced the solar year with the lunar months of the Islamic calendar, joining Hindu-Javanese and Islamic timekeeping.

jacques-duchesne.s: Jacques Duchesne was a French general who commanded the expedition that conquered Madagascar in 1895. Marching inland from Mahajanga with about 15,000 men, many of whom died of disease, he sent a flying column that reached Antananarivo and shelled it into surrender on 30…

jean-laborde.s: Jean Laborde was a French adventurer and industrialist who, shipwrecked on Madagascar in 1831, entered the service of Queen Ranavalona I. At Mantasoa he built a large industrial complex producing cannon, muskets, gunpowder, glass and soap, and in Antananarivo he built the…

joseph-francois-lambert.s: Joseph-François Lambert was a French merchant based in Mauritius who befriended Prince Rakoto, the future Radama II of Madagascar. In 1855 Rakoto granted him the Lambert Charter, sweeping rights to exploit land, minerals and timber, which he confirmed as king in 1862.

james-cameron-missionary.s: James Cameron was a Scottish artisan missionary of the London Missionary Society who worked in Madagascar from 1826 to 1835 and again from 1863 until his death. He introduced crafts such as brickmaking and soap production, and later designed churches and other stone buildings…

james-hastie.s: James Hastie was a British agent at the court of Radama I of Madagascar from 1817 until his death in 1826. Sent by Robert Farquhar, governor of Mauritius, he negotiated the Anglo-Merina treaties of 1817 and 1820 that ended the export of slaves in return for arms, training and…

jose-clemente-orozco.s: José Clemente Orozco was a Mexican painter, one of the three leading artists of the Mexican mural movement. His frescoes, darker and more critical than those of Rivera and Siqueiros, depict war, revolution and human suffering.

jose-lopez-portillo.s: José López Portillo was president of Mexico from 1976 to 1982. Huge oil discoveries in the Bay of Campeche financed a boom and heavy foreign borrowing under his government, but falling oil prices brought a debt crisis in 1982.

jose-vasconcelos.s: José Vasconcelos was a Mexican philosopher, writer and politician who, as secretary of public education from 1921 to 1924, built schools and libraries, sent teachers into the countryside and commissioned murals from Diego Rivera and other painters. His essay The Cosmic Race…

juan-rulfo.s: Juan Rulfo was a Mexican writer and photographer whose small body of work had great influence on Latin American literature. His story collection The Burning Plain (1953) and novel Pedro Páramo (1955), set among the dead of a ruined village in Jalisco, portray rural Mexico…

joseph-goebbels.s: Joseph Goebbels was a Nazi politician and Hitler's Minister of Propaganda from 1933 to 1945. As Gauleiter of Berlin and head of the Reich Chamber of Culture, he controlled the press, radio, film and arts, built up the cult of the Führer and stirred hatred of Jews.

james-wolfe.s: James Wolfe was a British army officer who commanded the expedition against Quebec in 1759 during the Seven Years' War. After a summer of failed attempts, his troops climbed the cliffs at the Anse au Foulon at night and defeated the French under the Marquis de Montcalm on the…

jeanne-mance.s: Jeanne Mance was a French nurse and settler who co-founded Ville-Marie, later Montreal, with Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve in 1642. She founded and ran the Hôtel-Dieu de Montréal, the city's first hospital, and helped to secure the funds and settlers that saved the…

jean-francois-de-la-rocque-de-roberval.n: Jean-François de La Rocque de Roberval
jean-francois-de-la-rocque-de-roberval.s: Jean-François de La Rocque de Roberval was a French nobleman and Protestant courtier whom Francis I appointed in 1541 as lieutenant-general of Canada to found a colony. Arriving in 1542, he wintered with his settlers at Cap-Rouge near present-day Quebec City, where many died…

jose-de-iturrigaray.s: José de Iturrigaray was a Spanish army officer and Viceroy of New Spain from 1803 to 1808. After Napoleon forced the Spanish Bourbons to abdicate in 1808, he appeared to favour criollo proposals for a provisional assembly in Mexico, and peninsular merchants led by Gabriel de…

jose-maria-morelos.s: José María Morelos was a Mexican priest and the leading commander of the War of Independence after the death of Miguel Hidalgo. He won control of much of southern Mexico, convened the Congress of Chilpancingo in 1813 and set out his programme in the Sentimientos de la Nación.

juan-diego.s: Juan Diego was a Nahua convert to whom, according to Catholic tradition, the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared on the hill of Tepeyac near Mexico City in December 1531. The image said to have been imprinted on his cloak became the focus of the Guadalupe devotion.

jenny-shipley.s: Jenny Shipley is a New Zealand politician who became the country's first woman Prime Minister in December 1997, after replacing Jim Bolger as leader of the National Party. Earlier, as social welfare minister in 1990–1991, she cut benefits as part of the National government's…

jim-bolger.s: Jim Bolger was Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1990 to 1997, leading the Fourth National Government. His government continued the free-market reforms begun by Labour, with welfare cuts and labour-market deregulation under finance minister Ruth Richardson.

jiaqing-emperor.s: The Jiaqing Emperor was emperor of the Qing dynasty of China from 1796 to 1820, succeeding his father, the Qianlong Emperor. He purged the corrupt minister Heshen and suppressed the White Lotus Rebellion, but faced growing financial strain and piracy along the coast.

jean-jacques-rousseau.s: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a Genevan-born philosopher, writer and composer whose works shaped the political thought of the Enlightenment and the French Revolution. In The Social Contract (1762) he argued that legitimate government rests on the general will of the people, and in…

johann-rudolf-wettstein.s: Johann Rudolf Wettstein was mayor of Basel from 1645 and the leading Swiss diplomat of his time. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 he obtained recognition that the Swiss Confederacy was exempt from the jurisdiction of the Holy Roman Empire, in effect its formal independence.

jacobus-boshof.s: Jacobus Boshof was the second president of the Orange Free State, from 1855 to 1859. Born in the Cape Colony, he had been an official in Natal before his election, and he gave the young republic firmer administration.

jagersfontein.s: Jagersfontein is a town in the south of the Free State province of South Africa, which grew around a diamond mine opened in the early 1870s. Its huge open pit, largely dug by hand, yielded the Excelsior diamond in 1893 and the Jubilee diamond in 1895.

jiang-qing.s: Jiang Qing was a Chinese actress and politician, the fourth wife of Mao Zedong. During the Cultural Revolution she led radical attacks on the arts and party officials and became the most prominent member of the Gang of Four.

jiang-zemin.s: Jiang Zemin was a Chinese Communist leader who became general secretary of the party after the Tiananmen Square protests of 1989 and served as president of the People's Republic from 1993 to 2003. His years in power saw rapid market-oriented growth, the return of Hong Kong and…

johannes-ciconia.s: Johannes Ciconia was a composer born in Liège who worked in Italy, above all in Padua, where he died in 1412. His motets, mass movements and secular songs combined French and Italian styles and made him one of the leading composers of the years around 1400.

juliana-of-cornillon.s: Juliana of Cornillon was an Augustinian nun near Liège whose visions led her to campaign for a feast honouring the Eucharist. Bishop Robert of Thourotte instituted the Feast of Corpus Christi in the diocese in 1246, and Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole church in 1264.

james-fitzjames-1st-duke-of-berwick.s: James FitzJames, 1st Duke of Berwick, was an illegitimate son of James II of England who became a marshal of France. In the War of the Spanish Succession he won the Battle of Almansa in 1707 and took Barcelona in September 1714 after a long siege.

johann-i-joseph-prince-of-liechtenstein.n: Johann I Joseph, Prince of Liechtenstein
johann-i-joseph-prince-of-liechtenstein.s: Johann I Joseph was prince of Liechtenstein from 1805 to 1836 and an Austrian field marshal who fought in the Napoleonic Wars and negotiated the Peace of Pressburg in 1805. Under him Liechtenstein became sovereign in the Confederation of the Rhine and then joined the German…

johann-ii-prince-of-liechtenstein.s: Johann II, called the Good, was prince of Liechtenstein from 1858 to 1929, one of the longest reigns in European history. He granted the constitution of 1862, disbanded the army in 1868, and approved the constitution of 1921; a great art patron, he gave many works to museums.

jinasena.s: Jinasena was a Digambara Jain monk and scholar of the ninth century, revered as teacher of the Rashtrakuta emperor Amoghavarsha I. He completed the Jayadhavala commentary on Jain scripture begun by his own teacher Virasena and began the Adipurana, the Sanskrit life of the…

jamaa-el-djedid.s: The Jamaa el Djedid, or New Mosque, is a mosque on the waterfront of Algiers, built in 1660 for the Hanafi rite followed by the Ottoman garrison and Turkish community of the Regency. Its large central dome and cross-shaped plan show Ottoman influence, combined with a square…

jose-ballivian.s: José Ballivián was a Bolivian general and president from 1841 to 1847. On 18 November 1841 he defeated a Peruvian invasion at the Battle of Ingavi, where the Peruvian president Agustín Gamarra was killed, securing Bolivia's independence.

jose-manuel-balmaceda.s: José Manuel Balmaceda was president of Chile from 1886 to 1891. He used nitrate revenue for public works, but his conflict with Congress over the budget led to the civil war of 1891, in which the navy and Congress defeated the army loyal to him.

joaquin-prieto.s: Joaquín Prieto was a Chilean general who led the conservative forces to victory at the Battle of Lircay in 1830. As president from 1831 to 1841, with Diego Portales as his leading minister, he presided over the Constitution of 1833 and the victorious War of the Confederation…

jose-joaquin-perez.s: José Joaquín Pérez was president of Chile from 1861 to 1871, the last of the four presidents who each served two consecutive five-year terms. A moderate conservative, he governed through broad coalitions and eased the conflicts left by the Montt era.

jaime-roldos-aguilera.s: Jaime Roldós Aguilera was a lawyer from Guayaquil who became the first president of Ecuador's restored democracy in 1979, after nearly a decade of military rule. His government promoted human rights in the region and faced a border war with Peru in 1981.

jamil-mahuad.s: Jamil Mahuad was mayor of Quito and president of Ecuador from 1998 to 2000. He signed the peace agreement of 1998 that ended the border dispute with Peru, but his government faced a severe banking collapse and froze bank deposits in 1999.

jorge-icaza.s: Jorge Icaza was an Ecuadorian novelist and playwright, a leading writer of the indigenista movement in Latin American literature. His novel Huasipungo of 1934 described the brutal exploitation of indigenous labourers on highland estates and was translated into many languages.

jose-maria-velasco-ibarra.s: José María Velasco Ibarra was the dominant figure in Ecuadorian politics for four decades, who held the presidency five times between 1934 and 1972 but completed only one full term, from 1952 to 1956. A charismatic populist orator, he was overthrown by the army four times, the…

juan-montalvo.s: Juan Montalvo was an Ecuadorian essayist and liberal polemicist, the fiercest critic of the Catholic conservative regime of Gabriel García Moreno and later of the dictator Ignacio de Veintemilla. After García Moreno's assassination in 1875 he reportedly declared 'my pen killed…

julian-revolution.s: The Julian Revolution was a coup carried out on 9 July 1925 by young officers of the Ecuadorian army who overthrew the government. It ended the dominance of the Liberal oligarchy and the private banks of Guayaquil over the state.

jose-napoleon-duarte.s: José Napoleón Duarte was a Salvadoran engineer and a founder of the Christian Democratic Party, three times mayor of San Salvador. Denied victory by fraud in the presidential election of 1972, he was arrested and exiled.

johan-laidoner.s: Johan Laidoner was an Estonian general who commanded the army in the War of Independence of 1918–1920. He again led the armed forces in 1924, when he suppressed a communist coup attempt, and from 1934, when he backed Konstantin Päts's authoritarian regime.

juri-vilms.s: Jüri Vilms was an Estonian lawyer and politician, one of the three members of the Salvation Committee that proclaimed Estonia's independence on 24 February 1918 and deputy head of the provisional government. In April 1918, while travelling to Finland on a mission abroad, he…

jean-sibelius.s: Jean Sibelius (1865–1957) was a Finnish composer whose seven symphonies, tone poems and the patriotic Finlandia of 1899 made him the leading figure of Finnish music and a symbol of national identity under Russian rule. Drawing on the Kalevala epic and the Nordic landscape, he…

juho-kusti-paasikivi.s: Juho Kusti Paasikivi (1870–1956) was a Finnish statesman who served as prime minister in 1944–1946 and as president from 1946 to 1956. A conservative banker and veteran negotiator with Moscow, who led the Finnish delegation at Tartu in 1920 and in the talks before the Winter…

john-hawkwood.s: John Hawkwood (c. 1323–1394) was an English mercenary captain who spent most of his career in Italy, leading the White Company and other bands for Pisa, Milan, the papacy and others.

jean-ii-le-maingre.s: Jean II Le Maingre (1366–1421), known as Boucicaut, was a Marshal of France and celebrated knight. Captured by the Ottomans at Nicopolis in 1396 and ransomed, he led an expedition to relieve Constantinople in 1399 and governed Genoa for the French crown from 1401 until a…

jimmy-morales.s: Jimmy Morales (born 1969) is a Guatemalan former television comedian who was president of Guatemala from 2016 to 2020. Elected as an anti-corruption outsider after the fall of Otto Pérez Molina, he turned against the International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala when…

jorge-serrano-elias.s: Jorge Serrano Elías (born 1945) is a Guatemalan politician who was elected president in 1991, succeeding Vinicio Cerezo in the first transfer of power between elected civilians in decades. On 25 May 1993 he suspended the constitution and dissolved Congress and the Supreme…

juan-gerardi.s: Juan Gerardi (1922–1998) was a Guatemalan Catholic bishop and human rights defender. As auxiliary bishop of Guatemala he led the church's Recovery of Historical Memory project, whose report Guatemala: Never Again, presented on 24 April 1998, attributed the great majority of…

julio-cesar-mendez-montenegro.s: Julio César Méndez Montenegro (1915–1996) was a Guatemalan lawyer and politician who served as president from 1966 to 1970, the only civilian to hold the office between 1954 and 1986. Elected for the Revolutionary Party, he accepted army control over security in return for…

jorge-ubico.s: Jorge Ubico (1878–1946) was a Guatemalan general who ruled as president from 1931 to 1944. He built roads and cut corruption but governed as a dictator, favoured the United Fruit Company and replaced debt peonage with a vagrancy law that forced indigenous people to work.

jacmel.s: Jacmel is a port city on the south coast of Haiti, founded by the French in 1698 and now capital of the Sud-Est department. In the nineteenth century it was one of the country's main coffee-exporting ports, and its merchant houses with iron balconies survive.

jean-baptiste-riche.s: Jean-Baptiste Riché (1780–1847) was a Haitian general who served as president from March 1846 until his death in February 1847. One of the elderly Black generals chosen by the mixed-race elite as figurehead presidents, he restored the constitution of 1816 and suppressed…

jean-louis-pierrot.s: Jean-Louis Pierrot (1761–1857) was a Haitian general who served as president from April 1845 to March 1846. A veteran of the Haitian Revolution, he was one of the aged Black generals installed by the mixed-race elite after the fall of Charles Rivière-Hérard.

juan-manuel-galvez.s: Juan Manuel Gálvez (1887–1972) was a Honduran lawyer and National Party politician who served as president from 1949 to 1954, succeeding the dictator Tiburcio Carías Andino, whose minister of war he had been. His government began a cautious modernisation, creating the Central…

juan-orlando-hernandez.s: Juan Orlando Hernández (born 1968) is a Honduran National Party politician who was president from 2014 to 2022. After the Supreme Court set aside the constitutional ban on re-election, he won a second term in 2017 in a disputed count followed by deadly protests.

janata-party.s: The Janata Party was an Indian political party formed in 1977 by the merger of opposition groups, from socialists to the Hindu nationalist Jana Sangh, to fight Indira Gandhi after the Emergency. It won the general election of March 1977 and formed the first national government…

janis-balodis.s: Jānis Balodis was a Latvian general who commanded the national army in the War of Independence of 1919–1920 and later served as minister of war. He supported Kārlis Ulmanis's coup of 1934 and became deputy prime minister, but was dismissed shortly before the Soviet occupation…

juan-bautista-sacasa.s: Juan Bautista Sacasa was a Nicaraguan Liberal physician and politician who led the Constitutionalist rebellion of 1926–1927 against the Conservatives. Elected president in 1932, he took office as the United States Marines withdrew, but real power passed to Anastasio Somoza…

jimmy-carter.s: Jimmy Carter was the 39th president of the United States, serving from 1977 to 1981. A Democrat from Georgia, he made human rights central to foreign policy, signed the Torrijos–Carter Treaties with Panama in 1977 and brokered the Camp David Accords between Egypt and Israel in…

javier-perez-de-cuellar.s: Javier Pérez de Cuéllar was a Peruvian diplomat who served as the fifth Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1982 to 1991. He helped negotiate the end of the Iran–Iraq War in 1988, the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan and the peace accords in El Salvador.

jose-carlos-mariategui.s: José Carlos Mariátegui was a Peruvian journalist and political thinker, regarded as one of the founders of Latin American Marxism. After years in Europe, he founded the journal Amauta in 1926 and the Peruvian Socialist Party in 1928, arguing that socialism in Peru should build…

jose-maria-arguedas.s: José María Arguedas was a Peruvian novelist, poet and anthropologist who, raised among Quechua-speaking communities in the Andes, became the leading writer of indigenous Andean life in Spanish. His novels, including Deep Rivers (Los ríos profundos, 1958) and All the Bloods…

jacques-lauriston.s: Jacques Lauriston was a French general and diplomat of Scottish descent and an aide-de-camp of Napoleon. In May 1806 he occupied Ragusa with French troops and withstood a siege by Russian and Montenegrin forces until relieved.

john-vorster.s: John Vorster was a South African politician who was prime minister from 1966 to 1978 and then state president until 1979. As minister of justice under Verwoerd he oversaw harsh security laws against the anti-apartheid movement.

julius-classicianus.s: Gaius Julius Alpinus Classicianus was the Roman procurator, or chief financial officer, of Britain appointed after Boudica's revolt of 60 or 61. A Gaul from the Rhineland, he reported to Nero that the harsh reprisals of the governor Suetonius Paulinus were prolonging the…

jazuliyya.s: The Jazuliyya was a Sufi tradition of Morocco that grew from the teaching of Muhammad al-Jazuli (d. c. 1465), author of the prayer book Dala'il al-Khayrat, within the wider Shadhili lineage.

julfa-nakhchivan.s: Julfa, known to Armenians as Jugha, is a town on the Aras river in Nakhchivan, now part of Azerbaijan. In the sixteenth century it was a prosperous Armenian merchant town trading in Persian silk.

jibin.s: Jibin was the Chinese name for a kingdom or region in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, usually identified with Gandhara and Kashmir. Chinese histories such as the Han shu record that a Saka king fled south across the Pamirs to rule Jibin after the Yuezhi displaced…

junnar.s: Junnar is a town in Pune district, Maharashtra, India, at the foot of the Western Ghats near the Naneghat pass. In the Satavahana and Kshaharata period it was a trading centre surrounded by more than two hundred rock-cut Buddhist caves, among the largest groups in India.

jand.s: Jand was a medieval town on the lower Syr Darya, in present-day Kazakhstan, on the frontier between the Islamic lands of Central Asia and the steppe. In the tenth and eleventh centuries it was a centre of the Oghuz Turks, and the Seljuk clan settled near it and adopted Islam…

jie-of-xia.s: Jie of Xia was, according to traditional Chinese histories, the last ruler of the Xia dynasty. He is portrayed as a cruel and extravagant tyrant who was overthrown by Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty, at the Battle of Mingtiao.

jind-kaur.s: Jind Kaur was the youngest wife of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and mother of Duleep Singh, the last ruler of the Sikh Empire. She acted as regent for her young son from 1843, and after the First Anglo-Sikh War the British removed her from power, imprisoned and exiled her.

jang-bogo.s: Jang Bogo was a Silla commander and merchant who served in the Tang army in China and returned home to fight the slave trade along the coasts. In 828 he founded the garrison of Cheonghaejin on Wando, from which he dominated shipping and trade between Silla, Tang China and Japan.

jijeung-of-silla.s: Jijeung was king of Silla from 500 to 514. He fixed the name of the state as Silla, adopted the Chinese-style title wang, meaning king, banned the burial of people with the dead and encouraged ploughing with oxen.

jindeok-of-silla.s: Jindeok was queen of Silla from 647 to 654, the second woman to rule the kingdom. She came to the throne during the rebellion of Bidam, which was put down by Kim Yu-sin.

jinseong-of-silla.s: Jinseong was queen of Silla from 887 to 897, the third woman to rule the kingdom. Her government's attempts to collect taxes from exhausted provinces set off peasant uprisings from 889, and warlords such as Gyeon Hwon and Gung Ye built their own states.

johnson-south-reef-skirmish.s: The Johnson South Reef skirmish was a naval clash on 14 March 1988 in the Spratly Islands of the South China Sea between Chinese and Vietnamese forces. Chinese ships opened fire on Vietnamese troops and transport vessels at the reef, killing 64 Vietnamese, and China took…

juan-velasco-alvarado.s: Juan Velasco Alvarado was a Peruvian general who seized power in a coup in October 1968 and ruled as president until other officers removed him in 1975. His Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces nationalised the International Petroleum Company and other foreign firms,…

juan-felipe-ibarra.s: Juan Felipe Ibarra was an Argentine soldier and caudillo who governed Santiago del Estero almost continuously from 1820 until his death in 1851. In 1820 he declared the province's autonomy from the Republic of Tucumán under Bernabé Aráoz.

james-madison.s: James Madison was the fourth president of the United States, from 1809 to 1817, and a principal author of the US Constitution and the Bill of Rights. With Alexander Hamilton and John Jay he wrote The Federalist essays in defence of the Constitution.

jaeren.s: Jæren is a flat coastal district of Rogaland in south-western Norway, south of Stavanger. Its fertile farmland made it one of Norway's richest agricultural areas from prehistoric times, and it is known for its long sandy beaches, its stone walls and its many Iron Age burial…

janiculum.s: The Janiculum is a long hill on the west bank of the Tiber in Rome, outside the ancient city's seven hills. In 1849 it was the scene of the fiercest fighting in Giuseppe Garibaldi's defence of the Roman Republic against the French, and a monument to Garibaldi and memorials to…

jai-singh-i.s: Jai Singh I, known as Mirza Raja, was the Kachwaha ruler of Amber in Rajasthan from 1621 and one of the leading generals of the Mughal Empire. Serving Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, he forced the Maratha leader Shivaji to accept the Treaty of Purandar in 1665 and then led an…

jai-singh-of-mewar.s: Jai Singh was the Maharana of Mewar, ruling from Udaipur, from 1680 to 1698. He succeeded his father Raj Singh I during the war against the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, with whom he made peace in 1681 by ceding several districts.

jethwa-dynasty.s: The Jethwas are a Rajput clan of Saurashtra, in Gujarat, and one of the oldest ruling families of the region. Their tradition traces their power far back; historically they held western Saurashtra from seats at Ghumli and later Ranpur and Chhaya, and from 1785 at Porbandar.

julio-argentino-roca.s: Julio Argentino Roca was an Argentine general and statesman, twice president of Argentina, from 1880 to 1886 and from 1898 to 1904. As minister of war he led the Conquest of the Desert of 1878–1879, which destroyed the independence of the Mapuche, Ranquel and other peoples of…

jindo-island.s: Jindo is an island off the south-western tip of the Korean peninsula, part of South Jeolla Province. In 1270–1271 it was the base of the Sambyeolcho rebels, who built the Yongjang fortress there and set up a rival Goryeo court until a Goryeo and Mongol force took it.

john-fenwick-quaker.s: John Fenwick was an English Quaker and former Parliamentarian soldier who bought Lord Berkeley's half of New Jersey in 1674 together with Edward Byllynge. Disputes over the purchase, which came to be held in trust for Byllynge's creditors, led to the creation of West Jersey…

jozsef-mindszenty.s: József Mindszenty was archbishop of Esztergom and primate of Hungary from 1945 and a cardinal from 1946. An outspoken opponent of communism, he was arrested in December 1948 and sentenced to life imprisonment after a show trial in 1949.

jorge-b-vargas.s: Jorge B. Vargas was a Filipino lawyer and politician who served as executive secretary to President Manuel Quezon.

jose-p-laurel.s: José P. Laurel was a Filipino lawyer, judge and politician who served as president of the Second Philippine Republic, the state created under Japanese occupation, from 1943 to 1945.

jose-tomas-boves.s: José Tomás Boves was a Spanish-born royalist commander in the Venezuelan War of Independence. Leading an army of llaneros, the horsemen of the plains, he turned the war into a brutal social conflict against the Creole elite and defeated Simón Bolívar at La Puerta in June 1814,…

jayadeva.s: Jayadeva was a Sanskrit poet of the 12th century, author of the Gita Govinda, a celebrated poem on the love of Krishna and Radha. Tradition places him at the court of the Sena king Lakshman Sena, though Odisha also claims him through the village of Kenduli.

jaghbub.s: Jaghbub is an oasis in eastern Libya near the Egyptian border. In 1856 the Senussi order moved its headquarters there, and its founder Muhammad ibn Ali al-Senussi was buried in its mosque.

jharkhand.s: Jharkhand is a state of eastern India, created from southern Bihar in 2000, with its capital at Ranchi. Much of it lies on the Chota Nagpur plateau and it is rich in coal, iron ore and other minerals.

javier-solana.s: Javier Solana is a Spanish Socialist politician who was Secretary General of NATO from 1995 to 1999 and the European Union's High Representative for foreign and security policy from 1999 to 2009. In that role he brokered the Belgrade Agreement of 2002, which kept Serbia and…

juan-prim.s: Juan Prim was a Spanish general and Liberal politician who led the Glorious Revolution of 1868 that overthrew Isabella II. As head of government he searched Europe for a new king, a search that helped spark the Franco-Prussian War, and secured the election of Amadeo of Savoy.

juan-bautista-topete.s: Juan Bautista Topete was a Spanish admiral who raised the fleet at Cádiz against Isabella II in September 1868, starting the Glorious Revolution. He served as navy minister in the governments that followed.

jakob-erhardt.s: Jakob Erhardt was a German missionary of the Church Missionary Society who worked with Johann Krapf on the East African coast from 1849. He visited the Shambaa kingdom of Kimweri ye Nyumbai and studied local languages.

johann-ludwig-krapf.s: Johann Ludwig Krapf was a German missionary of the Church Missionary Society who founded the first Protestant mission in East Africa at Rabai near Mombasa in 1846. He travelled inland, visiting the Shambaa court, and in 1849 became the first European to see Mount Kenya.

jafar-ibn-muhammad-al-hasani.s: Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Hasani was a descendant of the Prophet's grandson al-Hasan ibn Ali who took control of Mecca in the 960s, around the time the Fatimids conquered Egypt. He founded the line of Hasanid sharifs who governed the holy city, usually acknowledging whichever…

jeddah.s: Jeddah is a port city on the Red Sea coast of the Hejaz in Saudi Arabia. Made the port of Mecca by the caliph Uthman in the 7th century, it became the main gateway for pilgrims arriving by sea and a centre of Red Sea trade.

julfar.s: Julfar was a medieval port on the northern coast of the Oman peninsula, near modern Ras al-Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates. From the 14th to the 17th century it was a centre of pearling and of trade between the Gulf, India and East Africa, and it was briefly held by the…

jezzar-pasha.s: Jezzar Pasha, Ahmad Pasha al-Jazzar, was an Ottoman governor of Bosnian origin who ruled from Acre as governor of Sidon from 1775 until his death in 1804. Known as "the Butcher" for his cruelty, he built up Acre's fortifications, mosque and markets and dominated Palestine and…

james-frazer.s: James Frazer was a Scottish anthropologist and classical scholar, author of The Golden Bough, first published in 1890. His comparative study of magic, religion and myth argued that many societies had divine kings whose vigour was bound to the fertility of the land and who were…

jiang-wei.s: Jiang Wei was a general of Shu Han in the Three Kingdoms period of China. A Wei officer who joined Zhuge Liang in 228, he became Shu's chief commander and launched repeated northern campaigns against Wei that exhausted the state.

jimutavahana.s: Jimutavahana is a legendary Vidyadhara prince of Indian story, famed for his self-sacrifice. In the tale, told in the Kathasaritsagara and in King Harsha's 7th-century Sanskrit play Nagananda, he offers himself to the bird Garuda in place of a young serpent, and his compassion…

joseph-stalin.s: Joseph Stalin (1878–1953) was the leader of the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until his death. A Georgian Bolshevik, he rose through the post of general secretary of the Communist Party after Lenin's death and imposed forced collectivisation, rapid industrialisation and…

juan-esteban-montero.s: Juan Esteban Montero (1879–1948) was a Chilean lawyer and Radical politician who was elected president in October 1931 after the fall of the dictator Carlos Ibáñez del Campo. Unable to cope with the economic collapse caused by the Great Depression, he was overthrown on 4 June…

jameson-raid.s: The Jameson Raid was a failed armed incursion into the South African Republic (Transvaal) by about 600 men of the British South Africa Company under Leander Starr Jameson, from 29 December 1895 to 2 January 1896. Planned with Cecil Rhodes to spark a rising of the Uitlanders in…

jinno-shotoki.s: The Jinnō Shōtōki ('Chronicle of the Direct Descent of Gods and Sovereigns') is a history of Japan written by Kitabatake Chikafusa in 1339 and revised in 1343. Tracing the imperial line from the age of the gods, it argued that the Southern Court of Go-Daigo's descendants held…

jiangxi.s: Jiangxi is an inland province of south-eastern China, with its capital at Nanchang, centred on the basin of the Gan River and Poyang Lake, which drain into the Yangtze. A rich rice-growing region, it became famous for the porcelain of Jingdezhen.

jose-maria-chacon.s: José María Chacón was a Spanish naval officer and the last Spanish governor of Trinidad, appointed in the 1780s. He oversaw the settlement promoted by the Cedula of Population, which multiplied the island's population.

jingzhou.s: Jingzhou is a city on the Yangtze River in southern Hubei province, China. Near it lie the ruins of Ji'nancheng, usually identified as Ying, the capital of the State of Chu, and the area is rich in Chu tombs.

jose-maria-castro-madriz.s: José María Castro Madriz (1818–1892) was a Costa Rican lawyer and statesman who as president proclaimed the Republic of Costa Rica on 31 August 1848, and is honoured as its founder. A liberal, he promoted education and the press during his first term from 1847 to 1849 and…

jose-matias-delgado.s: José Matías Delgado (1767–1832) was a Salvadoran priest and politician honoured as the father of the nation of El Salvador. He was a leader of the independence movement from the San Salvador rising of 1811, opposed annexation to Agustín de Iturbide's Mexican Empire after 1821,…

jonesborough-tennessee.s: Jonesborough is a town in north-eastern Tennessee, founded in 1779 by North Carolina as the seat of Washington County and the oldest town in Tennessee. In 1784 delegates of the western counties met there and declared the State of Franklin, which made it its first seat of…

ju-county.s: Ju County, or Juxian, is a county in Rizhao, in south-eastern Shandong province, China. It occupies the site of Ju, capital of the State of Ju, a non-Zhou state of the Dongyi peoples conquered by Chu in 431 BCE.

jimo.s: Jimo was an ancient city of the State of Qi in eastern Shandong, near modern Qingdao, of which Jimo is now a district. In 284–279 BCE, when the State of Yan under Yue Yi had overrun almost all of Qi, Jimo held out under Tian Dan, who broke the siege with his famous attack of…

jose-cuero-y-caicedo.s: José Cuero y Caicedo was a churchman born in Cali who became bishop of Quito at the start of the 19th century. He supported the Quito autonomy movement and presided over the second junta and the State of Quito from 1811.

jiangsu.s: Jiangsu is a coastal province of eastern China, on the lower Yangtze and Huai rivers, with its capital at Nanjing. Its southern part, including Suzhou and Yangzhou on the Grand Canal, was for centuries one of the richest regions of China, a centre of silk, rice, salt and…

jing-ke.s: Jing Ke was a retainer of Crown Prince Dan of Yan who tried to assassinate King Zheng of Qin, the future First Emperor, in 227 BCE. Admitted to the Qin court with a map of Yan territory hiding a dagger and the head of a Qin defector, he failed and was killed.

jean-baptiste-jourdan.s: Jean-Baptiste Jourdan was a French general and Marshal of the Empire. He won the Battle of Fleurus in 1794, securing the Austrian Netherlands for the French Republic, and gave his name to the Jourdan Law of 1798 that introduced conscription.

jahangir.s: Jahangir was the fourth Mughal emperor, reigning from 1605 to 1627. The son of Akbar, born Prince Salim, he largely kept his father's system of government, made peace with Mewar in 1615 and received the English envoy Sir Thomas Roe.

jahangir-mirza.s: Jahangir Mirza was the eldest son of Timur and his intended heir. In the 1370s he was married to Khanzada, a princess of the Sufid dynasty of Khwarazm, as part of Timur's dealings with that state.

jamalul-alam.s: Jamalul Alam was sultan of Sulu from 1862 to 1881. In January 1878 he granted North Borneo to Baron Gustav von Overbeck and Alfred Dent in return for an annual payment, an agreement later taken over by the British North Borneo Company.

jolo.s: Jolo is the main town of the island of the same name in the Sulu archipelago of the southern Philippines. It was the capital of the Sulu Sultanate and a busy trading port, exporting pearls, sea cucumbers and birds' nests.

johann-reinhold-patkul.s: Johann Reinhold Patkul was a Livonian nobleman who led the opposition of the Baltic German nobility to Charles XI's reduction of their estates. Sentenced to death in Sweden, he fled and helped build the alliance of Saxony-Poland, Denmark and Russia that attacked Sweden in…

jerez-de-la-frontera.s: Jerez de la Frontera is a city in the province of Cádiz, Andalusia, Spain, near the Guadalete river. Under Muslim rule it was the town of Sharish, and Castile conquered it in the 13th century, after which it lay on the frontier with Granada.

jahwarid-dynasty.s: The Jahwarids (Banu Jahwar) were a family of Córdoban notables who governed the city as a council-led republic after the abolition of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031. The founder, Abu al-Hazm ibn Jahwar, and his successors ruled as administrators rather than kings and kept…

jeju-island.s: Jeju Island is a volcanic island off the southern coast of South Korea, the country's largest island, dominated by Mount Hallasan. It was the seat of the kingdom of Tamna before its absorption by Goryeo, and in 1273 the last Sambyeolcho rebels were crushed there.

james-dole.s: James Dole was an American businessman who founded the Hawaiian Pineapple Company in 1901 and became known as the 'Pineapple King'. He planted pineapples on Oahu, bought the island of Lanai in 1922 to turn it into a vast plantation, and promoted canned pineapple across the…

jim-taylor-patrol-officer.s: Jim Taylor was an Australian patrol officer in the Territory of New Guinea. In 1933 he and the prospector Michael Leahy led an expedition into the Wahgi Valley, revealing to outsiders the large populations of the New Guinea Highlands.

john-the-baptist.s: John the Baptist was a Jewish preacher active in the Jordan valley in the early 1st century CE, who called for repentance and baptised followers in the river, among them Jesus. Both the Gospels and Josephus record that Herod Antipas imprisoned and executed him, the Gospels…

josephus.s: Flavius Josephus was a Jewish historian and a former commander in the revolt against Rome. Captured in Galilee in 67 CE, he won the favour of Vespasian and wrote in Rome The Jewish War and Jewish Antiquities, histories of the Jews from the creation to the revolt of 66–73.

jasaw-chan-kawiil-i.s: Jasaw Chan K'awiil I was the ruler of the Maya city of Tikal, in modern Guatemala, from 682 to about 734. In 695 he defeated Calakmul, Tikal's great rival, ending a long period of eclipse, and he commemorated the victory on carved wooden lintels.

jalon.s: The Jalón is a river of north-eastern Spain, a right-bank tributary of the Ebro that rises in the province of Soria and flows north-east past Calatayud to join the Ebro near Zaragoza. Its valley carries the main route between the Ebro basin and the central Meseta, followed by…

jamaat-al-muslimeen.s: Jamaat al Muslimeen is a Muslim organisation in Trinidad and Tobago led for decades by Yasin Abu Bakr. On 27 July 1990 about a hundred of its members stormed the parliament building and the state television station in Port of Spain, holding Prime Minister A.

jonang.s: The Jonang is a school of Tibetan Buddhism that took its name from the monastery of Jonang in Tsang, founded in the late 13th century. Its great teacher Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen (1292–1361) developed the zhentong ('emptiness of other') doctrine, and the scholar Taranatha…

jonggen-khatun.s: Jönggen Khatun, known in Chinese sources as Sanniangzi, was a wife of the Tümed ruler Altan Khan. After his death in 1582 she married his successors in turn and became the real power among the Tümed, upholding the peace and frontier trade with the Ming that Altan Khan had…

jaalin.s: The Ja'alin are an Arab tribe of the Nile valley in northern Sudan, centred on the region of Shendi, who claim descent from al-Abbas, the uncle of the Prophet. Many became merchants trading across Sudan in the 19th century.

jadidism.s: Jadidism was a reform movement among the Muslims of the Russian Empire in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name comes from the 'new method' (usul-i jadid) of teaching reading, promoted by the Crimean Tatar Ismail Gasprinski from 1884.

john-glenn.s: John Glenn was an American astronaut and politician. On 20 February 1962, in the capsule Friendship 7, he became the first American to orbit the Earth, circling it three times; after splashing down in the Atlantic he was debriefed on Grand Turk.

john-lawson-explorer.s: John Lawson was an English explorer, naturalist and surveyor in the Carolinas. In 1700 and 1701 he travelled about 900 kilometres through the interior, and his book A New Voyage to Carolina (1709) described its land, plants, animals and Native peoples.

jebtsundamba-khutughtu.s: The Jebtsundamba Khutughtu is the title of the highest reincarnate lama of Mongolian Buddhism, head of the Gelug school in Mongolia. The line began with Zanabazar (1635–1723), son of the Tüsheet Khan, and from the third holder the incarnations were found in Tibet.

jochids.s: The Jochids were the descendants of Jochi, the eldest son of Genghis Khan, who received the western lands of the Mongol Empire. Jochi's son Batu founded the Golden Horde, and his descendants ruled the steppes from the Danube to Siberia.

jose-maria-paz.s: José María Paz was an Argentine general of the wars of independence and a leading commander of the Unitarian party in the civil wars. In 1829–1830 he took Córdoba and defeated Juan Facundo Quiroga at La Tablada and Oncativo, forming the League of the Interior.

juan-facundo-quiroga.s: Juan Facundo Quiroga was an Argentine caudillo from La Rioja and one of the most powerful Federalist leaders of the civil wars after independence. Defeated by José María Paz at La Tablada and Oncativo, he crushed the Unitarians at La Ciudadela in 1831.

jebel-ali.s: Jebel Ali is a port town on the coast of Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, about 35 kilometres south-west of the city centre. Its deep-water harbour, opened in 1979, is one of the largest man-made harbours in the world and the busiest port in the Middle East.

jean-francois-vonck.s: Jean-François Vonck was a Brussels lawyer who led the democratic faction in the Brabant Revolution of 1789 against the Habsburg reforms of Joseph II. His followers, the Vonckists, wanted to broaden political representation beyond the privileged estates, but they were defeated…

jeroboam-i.s: Jeroboam I was the first king of the northern Kingdom of Israel, reigning from about 931 to 910 BCE according to the Hebrew Bible. A former overseer of Solomon's forced labour, he fled to Egypt after rebelling and returned to lead the northern tribes in rejecting Solomon's son…

john-r-hodge.s: John R. Hodge was a United States Army general who commanded XXIV Corps in the Pacific War, including at Leyte and Okinawa.

james-busby.s: James Busby was a Scottish-born British official who served as the first British Resident in New Zealand from 1833 to 1840. With little real power, he encouraged northern Māori chiefs to adopt a national flag in 1834 and to sign the Declaration of the Independence of New…

jebusites.s: The Jebusites were, according to the Hebrew Bible, the Canaanite people who inhabited Jerusalem, then called Jebus, before King David captured it and made it his capital. The Bible lists them among the peoples of Canaan and says that some continued to live in the city…

janibek-khan.s: Janibek Khan was a descendant of Urus Khan of the White Horde who, with Kerei Khan, founded the Kazakh Khanate. Around 1458–1465 the two sultans broke away from Abu'l-Khayr Khan's Uzbek confederation with their followers and settled in the Chu valley in Moghulistan.

jnatrikas.s: The Jnatrikas were a Kshatriya clan of ancient north-east India, members of the Vajji confederacy, living at Kundagrama near Vaishali in modern Bihar. They are known mainly as the clan of Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara of Jainism, whose father Siddhartha was one of their chiefs.

james-ii-of-urgell.s: James II of Urgell was count of Urgell from 1408 and a great-grandson of Alfonso IV of Aragon. When Martin I died without an heir in 1410 he was the leading Catalan claimant to the Crown of Aragon, but the Compromise of Caspe chose Ferdinand of Antequera in 1412.

johann-matthias-von-der-schulenburg.s: Johann Matthias von der Schulenburg was a German soldier who served Saxony and other powers before becoming field marshal of the Republic of Venice in 1715. In 1716 he commanded the defence of Corfu against a large Ottoman army and fleet, which abandoned the siege after weeks…

janaka.s: Janaka is the name of the kings of Videha in Vedic and epic tradition. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad King Janaka hosts philosophical contests between Brahmin teachers, above all the sage Yajnavalkya, and is praised as a seeker of knowledge.

jalaram.s: Jalaram, known as Jalaram Bapa, was a Hindu saint of Virpur in Saurashtra, Gujarat, and a devotee of Rama. Around 1820 he founded a free kitchen (sadavrat) at Virpur that fed all comers regardless of caste, a tradition still continued at his temple, which has refused donations…

jiu-river.s: The Jiu is a river of south-western Romania, about 340 km long, that rises in the Southern Carpathians, cuts through them in a gorge and flows south across Oltenia past Târgu Jiu and Craiova to the Danube. Its upper valley, the Jiu Valley, was Romania's main coal-mining area,…

john-eliot-missionary.s: John Eliot (1604–1690) was an English Puritan minister in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, known as the "Apostle to the Indians". He learned the Massachusett language, preached to Native communities from 1646 and organised settlements of Christian Native people known as praying…

josiah-harmar.s: Josiah Harmar (1753–1813) was an American officer of the Revolutionary War who served as the senior officer of the United States Army from 1784 to 1791. In October 1790 he led an expedition of regulars and militia against the Miami and Shawnee towns near present-day Fort…

jiuquan.s: Jiuquan is a city in western Gansu province, China, in the Hexi Corridor. It was founded as a Han commandery in the late 2nd century BCE, and its name, meaning "Wine Spring", comes from a legend about the general Huo Qubing.

jodensavanne.s: Jodensavanne, the "Jewish Savanna", was a settlement of Sephardic Jewish planters on the Suriname River, south of Paramaribo. Granted privileges from the 1660s, the community built a self-governing town there with the Beracha ve Shalom synagogue, completed in 1685.

jie-people.s: The Jie were a non-Chinese people of northern China in the 4th century, probably of Central Asian origin and associated with the Xiongnu confederation, settled in Shanxi. Their leader Shi Le founded the Later Zhao state, which dominated northern China.

jabrin-castle.s: Jabrin Castle is a fortified palace near Bahla in the interior of Oman, built around 1670 by the Ya'aruba imam Bil'arab ibn Sultan. Unlike most Omani forts it was designed chiefly as a residence and centre of learning, with painted ceilings, carved woodwork and Arabic…

jinshin-war.s: The Jinshin War was a succession war fought in Japan in 672 after the death of Emperor Tenji. Tenji's brother Prince Ōama raised forces in the eastern provinces and defeated the court of Tenji's son, Prince Ōtomo, who took his own life.

je-khenpo.s: The Je Khenpo is the chief abbot of the Central Monastic Body of Bhutan and the country's highest religious authority. The office was created by Ngawang Namgyal, the Zhabdrung, in the seventeenth century as the religious half of Bhutan's dual system of government, alongside…

joshua-nkomo.s: Joshua Nkomo was a Zimbabwean nationalist who founded the Zimbabwe African People's Union (ZAPU) in 1961 and led it through the guerrilla war against white minority rule in Rhodesia. With Robert Mugabe he formed the Patriotic Front in 1976.

jin-song-wars.s: The Jin–Song wars were a series of conflicts fought from 1125 to 1234 between the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty and the Song dynasty of China. In the Jingkang incident of 1127 the Jin took the Song capital Kaifeng and captured two emperors, forcing the Song court south to Hangzhou.

jurchen-campaigns-against-the-liao-dynas.n: Jurchen campaigns against the Liao dynasty
jurchen-campaigns-against-the-liao-dynas.s: The Jurchen campaigns against the Liao dynasty were the wars of 1114–1125 in which the Jurchens of Manchuria under Wanyan Aguda rose against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty. Aguda founded the Jin dynasty in 1115 and, in alliance with the Song, took the Liao capitals; the last Liao…

jacobite-rising-of-1745.s: The Jacobite rising of 1745 was Charles Edward Stuart's attempt to regain the British thrones for his father James Francis Edward Stuart. Landing in Scotland, he took Edinburgh, won at Prestonpans and marched as far as Derby before retreating.

jacobite-rising-of-1715.s: The Jacobite rising of 1715 was an attempt by James Francis Edward Stuart, the Old Pretender, to take the British throne from George I. The Earl of Mar raised the Jacobite standard in Scotland, but the indecisive Battle of Sheriffmuir and the surrender at Preston in November…
